detail.name: AI
detail.summary: AI — crowd and companion intelligence for Forge games. Pure decision layers over injected world probes: personality brains (TraitBrain), cheap kinematic locomotion (GroundLocomotion), bubble separation (CrowdSeparation), client pose blending (SnapshotInterp), sight/hearing memory (Perception) and weighted spawn specs (MobCatalog). The engine answers "what is true"; these modules decide what to do.

detail.name: Ability
detail.summary: Ability — costs, cooldowns, cast windows and targeting. Everything a game calls a "skill", a "spell", an "attack" or a "tool use" is the same shape: check whether it can run, pay for it, wait a moment, then do something. Writing that shape once means a new ability is data plus one function, and it is impossible to forget the cooldown. Resources are not owned here. You register a resolver once and Ability stops caring whether stamina lives in a profile, a component or a table:
examples:
Ability.define("dash", {
cooldown = 4,
cost = { stamina = 24 },
targeting = "direction",
cast = 0,
run = function(ctx) ... end,
})
Ability.use("player:1", "dash", { direction = look })

Ability.resources(function(subject, kind) return pool(subject, kind) end,
function(subject, kind, amount) spend(subject, kind, amount) end)

detail.name: Access
detail.summary: Access — the game is playable by people this engine had not considered. Forge had none of this. Not a colour-blind palette, not a subtitle, not a way to make text bigger. On a platform whose audience is mostly young and mostly on a phone held at arm's length, that is not a nice-to-have that can wait for version three. Three things, in the order they matter: **Colour.** Roughly one man in twelve cannot reliably separate red from green, and this engine's damage numbers are red, its health bar is red, and its "good" is green. A palette swap fixes all of it at once because every colour in `UI.theme` is a token rather than a literal — which is the reason tokens were worth the trouble. **Subtitles.** Every audio cue that carries information — a boss telegraph, a warning, a line of dialogue — is information a deaf player does not get. `Audio` already names its cues; a subtitle is a caption on a name that already exists. **Text size.** A HUD readable on a monitor is not readable on a phone at arm's length, and Roblox's own accessibility setting is something a game has to honour deliberately. --- Why this is not a settings menu ------------------------------------- Because a setting nobody finds is a setting nobody uses. Everything here is applied by the engine to things the engine already owns: `UI` colours, an `Audio` cue, a `TextLabel`'s size. A game gets it by using the engine normally, and a game that wants a menu builds one over `Access.set`.
examples:
Access.palette("deuteranopia")
Access.caption("boss.telegraph", "The Hollowed King raises its arm")
Access.textScale(1.25)

functions.name: Access.palette
functions.summary: Apply a palette to the engine's theme. The original is captured on the first call so a return to `default` is a real restore rather than a second guess at what the colours were.

functions.name: Access.caption
functions.summary: Give an audio cue a caption. Keyed by the cue name `Audio` already uses, so a game that has named its sounds well has already done most of this work. A cue with no caption simply produces none — silence is the right default for a footstep.

functions.name: Access.announce
functions.summary: Announce a cue, if it has a caption and captions are on. `Audio` calls this on every play. The engine doing it means a game gets subtitles by naming its sounds, rather than by remembering to caption each one at each call site — which is how half of them end up uncaptioned.

functions.name: Access.textScale
functions.summary: Scale every piece of text the engine renders. Applied to `UI.theme.text` rather than to individual labels, so it reaches widgets built before the setting changed as well as after. Clamped because a scale of four is a HUD that covers the game.

functions.name: Access.followSystem
functions.summary: Roblox's own accessibility preference, honoured. `GuiService.PreferredTextSize` is a system setting the player already chose. A game that ignores it makes them choose twice, and most never find the second one.

functions.name: Access.reducedMotion
functions.summary: Turn the engine's own aggression down. `Feel` shakes the screen, tints it and stops time on a hit, and all three are causes of motion sickness. Read by `Feel` rather than enforced here, because a module that reaches into another to disable it is a module the next reader cannot follow.

functions.name: Access.motionScale
functions.summary: : What `Feel` should multiply its intensity by. One call, one number.

functions.name: Access.deserialize
functions.summary: Restore a player's choices. Accessibility settings belong in the save profile, not in a client-side preference: a player who set them up once should not do it again on their next device, and they are the settings a player is least willing to re-discover.

detail.name: Achievements
detail.summary: Achievements — a thing you did once, remembered for ever. Not quests, and the difference matters -------------------------------------- `QuestEngine` runs objectives that are given, tracked and completed, and a completed quest is over. An achievement is the opposite shape: nobody hands it out, it watches counters that already exist, it fires once in a player's lifetime, and it stays. "Kill 10,000 enemies" is not a quest anybody accepted; it is a number that eventually crosses a line. That difference produces the two properties everything here is built on: **Once, ever.** A player who has it does not get it again — not on rejoin, not when the counter passes the threshold a second time, not when an admin resets something. Awarding twice is worse than not awarding: it is silent inflation of whatever the reward was. **Retroactive.** A game adds an achievement for something players have been doing for months. Their counters already qualify. It must fire on next login, or the veterans — the people who most deserve it — are the only ones who never get it. Tiers, because one number is rarely one achievement -------------------------------------------------- Kill 100, 1,000, 10,000. Declared as one achievement with thresholds rather than three achievements, so the progress bar knows what the next rung is and the definition does not repeat itself twice.
examples:
Achievements.define("slayer", { stat = "kills", target = 10000 })
Achievements.evaluate(player, profile)   --> { "slayer" }

Retroactive by construction: it compares the counter against the tiers with no memory of when the counter moved, so an achievement added today fires tomorrow for everybody who already qualified.

Two hundred enemies become two hundred scheduler entries and a server that dies at forty. Here every actor is a table, every brain is a data-declared state machine, and all of them tick in one sliced group. Two hundred actors cost one connection and a quarter of them think per frame. The engine runs the machine. What the states mean is entirely yours.

It costs a path computation per repath, which is why it is not simply always on: a swarm of thirty melee enemies in an open arena gains nothing and pays for all of it. detail.name: Anim
detail.summary: Anim — layered procedural animation with markers. Why not AnimationTrack and rbxassetid ------------------------------------- Authored animation needs the Animation Editor and an upload, which means a human in a GUI for every timing change. That is fine for a studio and fatal for an agent: the one thing that most needs iteration becomes the one thing that cannot be iterated. Here a clip is *data*. It works on R6 and R15, it needs no asset, and — the part that actually matters — it carries its own MARKERS. The frame a sword becomes dangerous lives in the same table as the pose that swings it. Move the pose, the hit window moves with it. That is what makes combat timing tunable without touching combat logic. This does not replace authored animation. When you have a real animator, keep the clip names and the marker names and swap the pose source; every system that listened for "hit" still works. Track convention (degrees) -------------------------- swing   forward/back — the primary axis of a limb spread  outward, away from the body twist   rotation about the limb's own axis, or torso yaw Usage -----
examples:
local anim = Anim.new(character)
anim:setLocomotion(Anim.profiles.grounded)
anim:onMarker(function(clip, marker) ... end)

local playback = anim:play("attack_1", { speed = 1.2 })
Anim.bind(anim)   -- drives it on the right loop for this context

functions.summary: Movement that comes from the animation instead of from the controller. A dodge that plays a roll while the controller applies an impulse is two systems guessing at the same distance, and they disagree: the roll ends early, or the body slides past the end of it. Root motion makes the clip the authority — the animation says how far the body travels and the controller does nothing. A clip declares it as a curve of offsets in the character's own space: Applied as a delta each frame rather than an absolute position, so it composes with whatever else is moving the character and never teleports it back to where the clip thought it started.

detail.name: Areas
detail.summary: Areas — where a player is allowed to be, and where they wake up. Every game with more than one place to stand needs the same four answers, and every one of them gets rebuilt badly per game: which areas exist, and how they connect whether this player may enter this one yet where they were when they left where they respawn if the answer to the third is "somewhere they can no longer go" That last one is the one that bites. A player unlocks a zone, plays there, the zone is removed in an update or their unlock is revoked, and they respawn inside geometry that is no longer theirs — or worse, inside nothing at all. An area system that cannot answer "where should this player be *now*" is a fall through the world waiting to happen. Server-authoritative, and it has to be -------------------------------------- Entry is a permission, so it is decided where permissions are decided. A client that asks to teleport is asking, not telling: `enter` re-checks every time rather than trusting that the UI only offered legal doors.
examples:
Areas.mayEnter(player, "crystal_caves")   --> false, "needs level 12"
Areas.enter(player, "crystal_caves")
Areas.respawnFor(player)                  --> the best legal area

The cascade exists because every step of it happens: unlocks get revoked, areas get removed, and a player whose saved area no longer admits them still has to appear somewhere with a floor. Returns nil only when the game defines no safe area, which is a configuration error rather than a runtime one — and one worth finding at startup rather than at a respawn.

detail.name: Assets
detail.summary: Assets — one way to name and produce content. Without this every game invents its own loading: one system clones from ReplicatedStorage, another builds a rig from a table, a third has ids baked into an `if` chain. Then nothing can be listed, nothing can be preloaded, and a missing asset is a nil three frames later instead of a named error. Three things an asset id can resolve to, and Assets does not care which: a definition   a plain table (stats, config) a template     an Instance in the tree, cloned on demand a builder      a function that constructs it (procedural rigs, props) Namespaces ---------- An id is `Namespace.Name`, or `Namespace.Group.Name`. The namespace picks the producer, so registering a producer once teaches the engine how to make every asset of that kind: Missing assets never crash. They log once, and `spawn` returns a visible magenta placeholder — because a silent nil is how a level ends up with invisible holes nobody notices until a player falls through one.
examples:
Assets.spawn("Enemy.Orc", CFrame.new(0, 5, 0))
Assets.spawn("Prop.Barrel", cframe)
local sword = Assets.build("Weapon.Sword")

Assets.producer("Enemy", function(id, def) return Rig.build(def.rig) end)
Assets.register("Enemy.Orc", { rig = { scale = 1.2, shape = "biped" } })

detail.name: Audit
detail.summary: Audit — where the money comes from, where it goes, and how long it takes. The three questions nobody can answer about their own economy ------------------------------------------------------------- How long does it take a new player to afford the first upgrade? How long does it take a player at hour twenty? Is there anything to spend on at hour forty? Every economy is designed by writing prices and rewards into a table, and the table cannot be read for the answers. A price of 5,000 means nothing until you know that the thing next to it earns 40 a minute, at which point it means "two hours", at which point somebody says "that is too long" and the number changes. This is the module that turns the table into the sentence. Faucets and sinks, because that is what an economy is ---------------------------------------------------- A faucet puts currency in, a sink takes it out. An economy where the faucets outrun the sinks inflates until the numbers are meaningless; one where the sinks outrun the faucets is a grind nobody finishes. Neither is visible from any single number, and both are obvious the moment they are listed side by side. The two failures it names ------------------------ **Nothing to spend on.** A player past the last sink is still earning and has nowhere to put it. That is the moment a game stops having a loop, and it is invisible in a spreadsheet sorted by price. **A wall.** One sink that takes ten times longer than the one before it. Players do not experience a curve, they experience the step — and a step past about three times the previous gap reads as "the game wants money".
examples:
Audit.faucet("kill", { amount = 12, perMinute = 4 })
Audit.sink("sword", { price = 5000, tier = 1 })
Audit.report()   --> earns 48/min, the first sink is 1h 44m away

detail.name: AutoTarget
detail.summary: AutoTarget — which of these am I actually hitting? Not aggro, and not a hitbox --------------------------- `AggroTable` answers "who is the enemy angry at" — a server question about threat. `HitGeometry` answers "did this swing connect" — a geometry question about one attack. This answers the third question, which sits between them and is the one players feel: **out of everything in front of me, which one does the game think I mean.** Get it wrong and the game feels broken in a way nobody can articulate. The sword swings at the husk behind you instead of the one you are looking at. The heal goes to the full-health ally. The lock-on snaps to a corpse. The rule that makes it feel right --------------------------------- Distance alone is wrong, and it is what everybody writes first. The nearest enemy is frequently not the one you are facing, so a purely nearest-target system swings sideways at something behind your shoulder. Facing alone is also wrong: the thing you are most precisely aimed at may be forty studs away behind the one in your face. So it is both, weighted, with facing dominant — a target twenty degrees off and close beats one dead ahead and distant. That single weighting is the whole difference between combat that feels like it obeys you and combat that feels like it argues. Pure, and injected ------------------ It takes positions and returns a choice. No raycasts, no CollectionService, no Humanoid reads — the game supplies candidates, this decides among them, and the whole thing is testable with three vectors and no DataModel.

detail.name: Bench
detail.summary: Bench — measured cost, instead of a number from an empty room. Every performance figure this engine had came from a Studio session with one player standing still. That is not evidence about a server with thirty people and four thousand entities; it is evidence about an empty room. What this can and cannot measure -------------------------------- Roblox refuses to conjure a Player: `Players:CreateLocalPlayer` and `Instance.new("Player")` both fail on capability, which is measured and recorded in the platform notes. So this does not simulate clients. It simulates *load*: N moving anchors, N entities, N receivers for a proximity broadcast — the server-side costs that actually scale. Replication bandwidth and client frame time still need real players, and this module says so rather than implying otherwise.
examples:
Bench.run("entity.query.2000", function() ... end, 200)
Bench.suite()          -- the standard set
Bench.report()

functions.name: Bench.run
functions.summary: Run `fn` `iterations` times and report the distribution. Reports the median and the 95th percentile, not the mean. A mean hides the frame that took 40ms, and the frame that took 40ms is the one the player felt.

functions.name: Bench.anchors
functions.summary: Synthetic anchors, for streaming and proximity work. They move on separate circles at different speeds, because the interesting case is not "thirty players in one place" — it is thirty players spread out, each pulling a different chunk set, which is when a streamer thrashes.

detail.name: BigNumber
detail.summary: BigNumber — arbitrary-magnitude numbers in scientific notation, pure Luau. A value is a { mantissa, exponent } pair with the mantissa normalised into [-10, -1) ∪ [1, 10) (or exactly zero). Doubles saturate near 1e308; here the exponent keeps counting, which is what incremental-game economies need. Underflow collapses to zero. Growth past a configurable exponent ceiling (default 1000) caps there instead of escaping to infinity.
examples:
local price = BigNumber.new(1e15)
BigNumber.format(price)      --> "1.00Qd"
BigNumber.parse("1.00Qd")    --> the same value back

detail.name: Boot
detail.summary: Boot — a startup that waits for things instead of hoping about them. The bug this exists to make impossible -------------------------------------- Every startup race has one shape: a system starts, needs something that is not ready, and instead of *waiting for that thing* it does one of three losing moves — waits on a fire-once event that has already fired and hangs for ever, polls an attribute on a timer, or looks for a child and gives up if it is missing. All three are timing-driven, and timing-driven startups do not fail when you write them. They fail later, on a slower machine or a faster one, and the symptom is never where the cause is. This project has already paid for that twice: a `SubscribeAsync` called inline stopped a server's bootstrap dead *after* the world was built, so `CharacterAutoLoads` was never re-enabled and no player ever got a body — with no error anywhere. Two pieces, and the second is worth as much as the first: Why `await` returning instantly matters --------------------------------------- It is the whole difference between this and a `BindableEvent`. A late subscriber to a fire-once event waits for a signal that already happened, which is a hang rather than an error, and a hang in startup looks exactly like a slow machine. A latch has no such state: it is either set, in which case you continue, or it is not, in which case you wait for it to be. The usage rule -------------- Never `await` inside a system's `start()`. That blocks the loader and turns one slow milestone into a dead server. Await inside a `task.spawn`:
examples:
Boot.signal("world_ready")            -- idempotent; second call is a no-op
Boot.await("world_ready", 30)         -- instant if already signalled

task.spawn(function()
Boot.await("models_ready")
dressTheWorld()
Boot.signal("world_dressed")
end)

functions.name: Boot.signal
functions.summary: Mark a milestone reached. Idempotent, on purpose. Startup code gets called twice more often than anyone expects — a retry, a second consumer, a system that starts itself defensively. A signal that throws or double-fires on the second call turns that into a bug; one that shrugs turns it into nothing.

functions.name: Boot.await
functions.summary: Wait for a milestone, or return immediately if it has already happened. Returns whether it was reached. A false means the timeout ran out, which the caller can act on — the point of a bounded wait is that "it never happened" is an answer rather than a hang.

functions.name: Boot.onReady
functions.summary: Do something once a milestone lands, without blocking the caller. The safe form of `await`, and the one a system's `start()` should use. It is `task.spawn` plus the wait, which is the pattern everybody writes by hand and half of them write wrong.

functions.name: Boot.awaitAll
functions.summary: Wait for several milestones at once. Sequential rather than parallel because they are latches: waiting for A then B costs the same as waiting for both, and the sequential form is one loop instead of a counter and a signal.

functions.name: Boot.declare
functions.summary: Say which milestone depends on what, and who is supposed to produce it. The declaration is the value. Without it a missing producer is a race that shows up on someone else's machine; with it, `validate` says so at startup in one line naming the milestone and the system that owed it.

functions.name: Boot.validate
functions.summary: Check the graph is honest before anything runs on it. Two faults, both of which are silent races at runtime and loud sentences here: a milestone that something requires and nobody produces, and a cycle. Returns the list of problems rather than throwing, so a caller can decide whether a half-declared graph is worth starting.

functions.name: Boot.mirror
functions.summary: Mirror the milestones where a client can read them. A loading screen that polls the world for symptoms — is the terrain there yet, are there any props — is guessing, and it guesses wrong the moment the world changes shape. Reading the server's own account of what is ready is the same information without the guess.

functions.name: Boot.reset
functions.summary: : For tests, which need a startup that has not happened yet.

detail.name: Builders
detail.summary: Builders — idempotent find-or-create helpers for code-built worlds. Worlds built from scripts must be rebuildable: every helper looks for the instance first and creates it only when missing, so running the builder twice yields one world, not two. Physical defaults live here so no builder invents its own.

functions.name: Builders.ensurePart
functions.summary: Creates or updates a part; returns (part, created).

detail.name: Camera
detail.summary: Camera — where the player is looking, and who decides. Forge had no camera at all. `Feel` shakes one and that was the entire surface, which means every game built on this engine had Roblox's default follow camera and no way to tell a story with it: no cutscene, no shoulder framing for a shot, no pull-back when something big arrives. The design is one idea: **modes stack, and the highest priority wins.** A cutscene does not have to know what the aim mode was doing, and the aim mode does not have to be cancelled — it is simply outranked, and returns the moment the cutscene releases. Anything else turns into a pile of booleans that eventually disagree. --- Why this fights Roblox's camera, and how ----------------------------- The default camera script writes `Camera.CFrame` every frame during the `Camera` render step. Anything written before that is overwritten, which is a mistake this project has already made once with an animator. So this binds *after* that step, and when a mode takes over it sets `CameraType = Scriptable` so Roblox stops writing at all. Releasing every mode hands control back rather than leaving the camera frozen where the last one left it, which is the other classic bug: a cutscene that ends and never gives the player their view back.
examples:
Camera.mode("shoulder", { priority = 10, ... })   -- while aiming
Camera.mode("cutscene", { priority = 100, ... })  -- during a scene

functions.name: Camera.mode
functions.summary: Add or replace a mode. Re-registering a name replaces it rather than stacking, so a system that updates its own mode every frame does not accumulate hundreds.

functions.name: Camera.impulse
functions.summary: A kick, in camera space. Recoil, a heavy landing, a hit taken. Additive on top of whatever mode is winning, so it works during a cutscene and during ordinary play without either knowing about it.

functions.name: Camera.shoulder
functions.summary: Over the shoulder. The framing every third-person shooter uses, and the one Roblox's default camera cannot do: the character sits off-centre so the crosshair is not behind their head.

functions.name: Camera.shot
functions.signature: Camera.shot(from: any, at: any, options: any?)
functions.summary: Look at something, from somewhere. The building block of every cutscene: a fixed shot. `from` and `at` may be values or functions, and the function form is what makes a shot follow something that is moving.

functions.name: Camera.cutscene
functions.summary: Play a sequence of shots, then give the camera back. Returns a handle with `skip`, because a cutscene a player cannot skip is a cutscene they resent on the second viewing. The camera is released when the sequence ends *or* is skipped — releasing in only one of those paths is how a game leaves someone stuck staring at a wall.

detail.name: Capability
detail.summary: Capability — ask Roblox what exists instead of assuming. This module exists because of a specific, expensive afternoon. `Sky.install` set `Terrain.Decoration = true`. That property does not exist in every Roblox version; on 0.735 it throws. Because `install` is a straight run of property writes, that one line aborted everything after it — the water never got its reflectance and a warning nobody saw never printed. A cosmetic nicety silently took out the rest of the function, and the only symptom was that the world looked slightly wrong. Then the same shape of bug happened three more times in a row with audio: invented marketplace ids, then `rbxasset://` names written from memory. Each one compiled, passed the doctor, passed the tests, built cleanly, and failed at runtime in front of a person. The pattern is always the same. Code written from memory about what the platform offers is a guess, and a guess that survives every static check. --- What this does ----------------------------------------------------- `set` writes the property if it exists and records the miss if it does not. Nothing throws, nothing aborts the caller, and `Capability.missing()` lists everything this build refused so it can be reported rather than discovered. --- Where the answers come from ---------------------------------------- Probes are cheap and cached: the first question about a property costs one pcall, every later one is a table lookup. `forge capability probe` runs the same checks from outside and writes them to JSON, so an agent can read what this Roblox build supports *before* writing code against it — which is the whole point.
examples:
Capability.has("Terrain.Decoration")   -- false on this build
Capability.set(Workspace.Terrain, "Decoration", true)  -- safe either way

functions.name: Capability.hasProperty
functions.summary: Does `Class.Property` exist on this build? Answered by reading the property off a real instance and catching the throw. Roblox exposes no reflection to a normal script, so a read that does not error is the only available proof that a name is real.

functions.name: Capability.hasClass
functions.summary: Can this class be created at all? New classes appear and old ones are retired. `Instance.new` on a name this build does not know throws, which is a slower answer than a lookup but a definitive one.

functions.name: Capability.has
functions.summary: Answer for a key already probed, without needing the instance to hand.

functions.name: Capability.set
functions.signature: Capability.set(instance: Instance, property: string, value: any)
functions.summary: Write a property, or record that this build does not have it. The replacement for a bare assignment anywhere the property is optional. The important part is not that it avoids the error — it is that the caller *continues*, so one missing cosmetic property can no longer take out the twenty lines after it. Returns whether the write landed, for the callers that care.

functions.name: Capability.get
functions.signature: Capability.get(instance: Instance, property: string, fallback: any?)
functions.summary: Read a property, or a fallback. The read side of the same problem: `Lighting.Technology` cannot be read by a plain script at all, and code that assumed it could spent a while reporting nonsense about the lighting model.

functions.name: Capability.missing
functions.summary: Everything this build refused. Worth surfacing rather than swallowing: a game silently missing its grass because one property vanished in a Roblox update is a bug that hides for months. This turns it into a line in the snapshot.

functions.name: Capability.prime
functions.summary: Load answers gathered outside the game. `forge capability probe` writes a table of what this Roblox build supports; feeding it in here means the first frame already knows, instead of learning one pcall at a time.

detail.name: CardCycle
detail.summary: CardCycle — deterministic deck / hand / next-card rotation. The Clash-style hand is four cards plus a preview of the fifth; playing a card slides `next` into the hand and pulls a fresh preview. When the draw pile runs dry the discard reshuffles with the same seeded stream, so two clients replaying the same seed see identical cycles forever.
examples:
local cycle = CardCycle.new({ cards = deckIds, handSize = 4, seed = 7 })
local result = cycle:play(cycle:hand()[1])

detail.name: Catalog
detail.summary: Catalog — Creator Store models this project has verified. Generated by `forge toolbox curate`. Do not hand-edit; regenerate it. Where these came from matters as much as what they are. They are not search results: each one was taken from a pack that Roblox developers actually use, found by reading the developer forum, and the pack's creator, licence and source thread travel with every piece. Most of them are Synty — a professional low-poly studio whose packs Roblox paid to release free, under an official Roblox account. Every entry was loaded inside Studio, measured and scanned. `parts`, `meshes` and `size` are readings off the real thing after insertion, not descriptions. Every entry has no scripts, because anything carrying one was refused rather than stripped: free-model scripts are the most common way a Roblox game gets backdoored, and deciding automatically which ones a model "needs" is exactly how that ships. An id absent from this file has not been checked, and `Assets` refuses it.
examples: local Catalog = Forge.Catalog

local trees = Catalog.byCategory("foliage")
local model = Catalog.load(trees[1])

functions.name: Catalog.verifiedPack
functions.summary: Whether a pack id may be inserted at all. `Assets` calls this before anything reaches the world, which is what stops an invented id from reaching a player.

functions.name: Catalog.kitShelf
functions.summary: What is on one shelf of the harvest. The harvester writes into `harvest/<category>/`, so the folder name *is* the category and asking the kit is cheaper and truer than keeping a manifest in Luau that drifts from the files on disk.

functions.name: Catalog.kitShelves
functions.summary: - Every category any mounted kit has anything on.

functions.name: Catalog.kitPieces

detail.name: ClassRegistry
detail.summary: ClassRegistry — declarative class movesets with fail-loud validation. Mines Fighting-game's ClassData (walk speeds, health pools, staminas, ability names with cooldowns) into one registrable shape. register() rejects malformed definitions immediately — a nil cooldown discovered mid-fight costs far more than an assert at boot. Registering the same class id twice is treated as programmer error, never a silent overwrite. Pure data: no Instances, no services.

detail.name: Clock
detail.summary: Clock — one time, agreed on by every server and every client. Why a game needs this and `os.time()` is not it ---------------------------------------------- `os.time()` is the machine's clock, and a live game runs on dozens of machines. Three questions break immediately without a single answer: **When does "today" end?** A daily reward that rolls over at the player's local midnight rolls over at a different moment for every player, and one who flies to Tokyo claims twice. Days are UTC or they are not days. **What is today's shop?** Two servers rolling their own random stock give two players different shops on the same day, and the first thing they do is compare screenshots. A day plus a salt seeds it, and every server on Earth derives the same list without talking to any other. **Has this expired?** A buff stored as "twelve hours from now" is stored against whichever clock wrote it. Stored as an absolute UTC instant, it means the same thing when it is read. Clients and drift ----------------- `Clock.sync` hands a client the server's time along with the round trip, so the client can hold its own offset and stop asking. It is not precision timing — it is close enough that a countdown does not disagree with the server by a visible second, which is the only thing anybody notices.
examples:
Clock.now()                          -- server time, one source
Clock.dayNumber()                    -- UTC day, the rollover unit
Clock.untilNextDay()                 -- for a countdown that is honest
Clock.dailySeed("shop")              -- same everywhere, all day
Clock.expiresIn(3600)                -- an absolute instant, not a duration
Clock.hasExpired(stamp)

functions.name: Clock.now
functions.summary: The time, as the server understands it. `os.time()` rather than `tick()` or `os.clock()`: this is a wall-clock instant that gets written to a DataStore and read back next week, and the other two are process-relative and meaningless the moment the server dies.

functions.name: Clock.precise
functions.summary: The same instant with sub-second resolution, for measuring rather than storing. Never persist this — `os.clock` is uptime, not a date.

functions.name: Clock.dayNumber
functions.summary: Which UTC day it is, as a whole number. The rollover unit for everything daily. Comparing day numbers is how you ask "is this from today" without any date arithmetic, and it is stable across servers because UTC is the same everywhere by construction.

functions.name: Clock.untilNextDay
functions.summary: Seconds until the next UTC midnight. For a countdown a player can trust. Computed from the day boundary rather than counted down in a loop, so a server that stuttered for four seconds still says the right thing.

functions.name: Clock.dailySeed
functions.summary: A number that is the same on every server all day, and different tomorrow. The mechanism behind a daily shop, a rotating quest set, a featured item: seed a `Random` with this and every server independently produces the same list. No messaging, no shared state, no drift — the day and the salt are the only inputs, and both are already agreed. The salt keeps unrelated systems from rotating in lockstep. Without it the shop, the quests and the featured pet all roll the same sequence and a player notices the pattern within a week.

functions.name: Clock.dailyRandom
functions.summary: : A `Random` already seeded for today. The form most callers actually want.

functions.name: Clock.weekNumber
functions.summary: Which week it is, counted from a UTC Monday. Unix epoch day 0 was a Thursday, so the shift by four is what makes weeks start on Monday rather than three days into one.

functions.name: Clock.expiresIn
functions.summary: Turn a duration into an instant. Storing "3600" means "an hour from whenever this is read", which is a bug that only appears after a restart. Storing the instant means the same thing for ever.

functions.name: Clock.remaining
functions.summary: : Seconds left, never negative — a countdown that goes below zero renders as : "-00:03 remaining" and every UI has to clamp it anyway.

functions.name: Clock.format
functions.summary: `1h 04m`, for a UI. Two units, largest first: `2d 06h` rather than `2d 6h 14m 3s`. A countdown with four units is read as noise, and the last two never matter at the moment somebody is looking at the first.

functions.name: Clock.stamp
functions.summary: What the server sends a client so it can stop asking. The round trip is included so the client can allow for the half of it that the answer spent in flight.

functions.name: Clock.adopt
functions.summary: Adopt the server's clock on a client. `roundTrip / 2` is the standard approximation: the answer is that old by the time it arrives, assuming the trip was symmetric. It is not, quite, but the error is milliseconds and the thing being corrected is a clock that could be minutes out. Refused on the server, where adopting an offset would mean the authority deferring to somebody else's idea of the time.

detail.name: Cluster
detail.summary: Cluster — the engine stops assuming there is one server. Everything Forge did before this ended at the edge of a session. `Save` had a session lock but nothing to coordinate with; `LiveOps` polled a DataStore on a timer because it had no way to be *told*; a leaderboard could only ever rank the twelve people in the room. None of that reads as a bug from inside one server, which is exactly why it survived: a single-server assumption is invisible until the day the game has two. Two Roblox services do the work, and they are for different things: `MessagingService` is a shout. Fire-and-forget, roughly a second of latency, no history, no delivery guarantee. Right for "a boss just spawned in server 12" and for pushing a config change that would otherwise wait a minute for the next poll. `MemoryStoreService` is shared *state*. Fast, transactional, and it expires. Right for a matchmaking queue, a global counter, a live-event total that every server contributes to. Using one where the other belongs is the classic mistake. A queue built on messages loses players; a shout built on a memory store polls forever. --- Limits that are real ------------------------------------------------ Roblox rate-limits both services per universe, and exceeding the limit drops calls rather than erroring. So every publish here goes through a token bucket sized under the documented ceiling, and a message that cannot be sent now is queued rather than lost. A cross-server layer that silently drops under load is worse than none, because it works in testing.
examples:
Cluster.on("boss.spawned", function(payload, fromServer) ... end)
Cluster.shout("boss.spawned", { name = "Hollowed King" })

Cluster.queue("ranked"):push(player.UserId, { rating = 1400 })
local party = Cluster.queue("ranked"):take(4)
Cluster.counter("event.shards"):add(12)

functions.summary: Tell every other server something. Rate-limited and queued rather than sent immediately, because Roblox drops calls past the limit instead of refusing them. Returns whether it went out now; either way it is either delivered or reported dropped, never silently lost.

functions.summary: Claim up to `count` entries. Returns the entries and a `confirm` function. Nothing is removed from the queue until `confirm` is called, so a server that fails to build the match releases the players back rather than losing them. Calling `confirm` is the promise that the match happened.

detail.name: Collab
detail.summary: Collab — more than one person editing without ruining each other's work. The Editor has always assumed a single author. Two people in the same session both grab the same rock, both move it, and the second write wins silently — no conflict, no warning, and the first person's work is simply gone. That is the failure that makes teams stop using a tool. Three mechanisms, in the order they matter: leases    one editor owns a placement at a time, and the claim expires presence  everyone can see who is here and what they are holding journal   every change is attributed, so a mistake can be traced --- Why leases rather than locks ----------------------------------------- A lock is held until released, which means a lock is held forever the first time somebody's Studio crashes while holding one. A lease expires. Editors renew what they are actively using and everything else falls free on its own, so the recovery path for a crash is "wait twenty seconds" rather than "find an administrator". --- Authority ------------------------------------------------------------- Server only, and every function refuses to run on a client. A lease that a client could grant itself is not a lease, and the whole point is to be the one place that arbitrates between two people who both want the same thing.
examples:
if Collab.claim(player, placement) then
Editor.setCFrame(placement, target)
Collab.record(player, "move", placement)
end

functions.name: Collab.keyFor
functions.summary: A stable name for the thing being edited. Placements carry an id; instances are identified by their full path. Both are strings, which is what lets one table arbitrate over both without knowing which kind of editor is asking.

functions.name: Collab.claim
functions.summary: Take ownership, or find out who has it. Re-claiming something you already hold renews it rather than failing: an editor dragging a rock calls this every frame, and a claim that refused its own owner would make dragging impossible.

functions.name: Collab.startSweeper
functions.summary: Drop leases nobody renewed. Without this, every crashed or disconnected editor leaves its work locked until the server restarts, which in practice means people work around the system rather than with it.

functions.name: Collab.here
functions.summary: Who is editing, and what they are looking at. Cheap and worth far more than it costs: most collisions are avoided by knowing somebody else is already in that corner of the map, long before any lease has to refuse anything.

functions.name: Collab.record
functions.signature: Collab.record(player: Player, action: string, subject: any, detail: any?)
functions.summary: What changed, by whom. Not undo — the Editor has its own stack for that. This is the answer to "who moved the spawn point", which on a team is asked far more often and is otherwise unanswerable.

detail.name: Combat
detail.summary: Combat — mechanism for hurting things. Never policy about what hurting means. The distinction is the whole design. Combat knows how to find what is in front of a sword, how to run a damage number through a chain of modifiers, how to keep a status effect ticking and how to fly a projectile. It does not know what armour is, whether crits exist, or how your game scales damage by level — you install those as modifiers, and they compose. Then a hit is: Modifiers run in ascending order. Order is explicit because "armour before or after crit" changes balance and should never be an accident of table iteration.
examples:
Combat.addModifier("armor", 100, function(ctx)
local armor = ctx.target:GetAttribute("Armor") or 0
ctx.amount *= 100 / (100 + armor)
end)

Combat.addModifier("crit", 200, function(ctx)
if ctx.rng and ctx.rng:bool(ctx.critChance or 0) then
ctx.amount *= 1.85
ctx.crit = true
end
end)

local hits = Combat.arc(root.Position, look, { range = 9, angle = 110 })
for _, model in hits do
Combat.damage(model, { amount = 24, source = player, critChance = 0.1 })
end

detail.name: ComboSequencer
detail.summary: ComboSequencer — data-driven attack chains with input buffering. Steps are inert data ({name, damage, windup, recovery, nextWindow}); the sequencer owns none of their meaning. Late presses are buffered for `bufferWindow` seconds (Fighting-game waits out the current swing instead of dropping inputs) and chains decay after `resetTimeout` seconds without an accepted link — SwordDude resets its combo after 0.5 s. Passing the final step wraps to the first, matching ChangeCombo; set loop = false to end chains there instead. Timing of windup/recovery/nextWindow stays with the caller — it decides when to call advance; the sequencer only judges whether a press links.

detail.name: Companion
detail.summary: Companion — things that follow you, and stay readable while they do. Pets, drones, hired workers, a bodyguard, a squad. The genre changes and the problems do not: where does each one stand, what does it do while nothing is happening, and how does it get there without fighting physics. Generalised from a shipped simulator, which is where the parts that are not obvious come from: * followers are sorted **small to front** and spaced by their own * the idle wander waits on the **leader's** stillness, not the follower's, * crowding is resolved by **pushing targets apart**, never by collision, Three things that system knew and this deliberately does not do -------------------------------------------------------------- **No physics.** The version this comes from began as one cloned script per follower driving unanchored parts on the server, and its own config carries the warning: several active at once "tanks server FPS". Formation maths returns offsets; moving something is the caller's, on the client, where a cosmetic follower belongs. **No teleport watchdog here.** That system needed one -- followers fell off the map, and the comment records it as a bug that survived ten months. A watchdog belongs to whatever owns the parts, because only that knows what "lost" means for its own world. **No ownership of what a follower *is*.** Its power, its rarity, its inventory slot: that is the game's, and a follow system that also owned those would be a pet system rather than a companion one.
examples: local Companion = Forge.Companion

local slots = Companion.Formation.resolve(followers, { mode = "risers" })
local dx, dz = Companion.Meander.step(state, dt, stillFor, busy)
footprint, so one large member does not eclipse or shoulder the rest;
and surrenders the instant the leader moves;
so the mover keeps sole control of the parts.

detail.name: DamagePipeline
detail.summary: DamagePipeline — pure resolution of a landed strike, nothing attached. Takes the move and both fighters as plain data and answers what the strike meant: full hit, blocked, miss or immune. Mines Fighting-game's HitHandler: i-frames beat everything except ignoreIframes, strikes from behind slip past guard, blocks bleed 20% chip (minimum 1), guardbreak shatters the block for x1.15 damage and a fixed 2 s stun, and superArmor never softens damage — it only refuses stun and knockback. Rule order is deliberate: 1. attacker incapacitated   -> miss   (a stunned attacker lands nothing) 2. victim i-frames active   -> miss   (unless move.ignoreIframes) 3. victim already dead      -> immune (corpses take no further damage) 4. guardbreak against block -> hit    (broken guard, fixed stun, x1.15) 5. block holds              -> blocked (chip damage + blockstun) 6. nothing applied          -> hit    (full damage) Facing convention: facingDot = dot(victimLook, dirToAttacker), so > 0 means the attacker stands in front of the victim and < 0 behind them. Pure in, pure out: no Instances, no services, no clocks. Numeric i-frame timestamps need `now`; without one they are treated as still active (fail-safe for server validation).

detail.summary: Data — content tables with a declared shape. Balance lives in data, not in code. That is easy to say and hard to keep: six weeks in, half the numbers are inline in a system somewhere and the other half are in a table nobody validates, so a typo'd `dmg` silently becomes `nil` and a sword does zero damage in production. rarity  = { type = "string", oneOf = { "common", "rare", "epic" } },

detail.name: Debug
detail.summary: Debug — how a running game explains itself. This is the seam between the two halves. The Quality Engine's bridge can already measure geometry: raycasts, bounds, overlaps, part counts. What it cannot see is *meaning* — whether the economy is solvent, whether forty actors are stuck in one state, whether anyone has taken damage in the last minute. Those are facts only the game knows. Debug makes the game say them out loud, in JSON, through a replicated StringValue the plugin can read while the place is running. No loadstring, which does not exist in a play session anyway. Then from the validator, with a command that already exists: It also carries live tunables, so a number can be changed in a running session and the effect observed without a rebuild — the shortest iteration loop the platform allows.
examples:

properties = { "Value" } }

functions.name: Debug.ready
functions.summary: Say the game has finished starting. Every automated look at a running game -- screenshots, interface measurement, the quality gate -- has to answer "is it up yet", and until now each of them guessed. The guesses were all versions of watching the HUD stop changing, and they were all wrong in the same way: a heads-up display builds its labels in the first frame and fills them as answers arrive, so anything watching it settles while the readout still says "Locating" and the player is still unarmed. A game whose server spends twelve seconds carving terrain was therefore photographed at second two, every time, and every absence in that photograph was read as a bug. Several were investigated. None existed. One line at the end of a bootstrap ends that whole category. What cannot be inferred from outside is trivially known from inside.

functions.name: Debug.expose
functions.summary: Publishes the game's self-description where a validator can read it. This is a StringValue, not a BindableFunction, and the reason matters: **a BindableFunction does not cross the client/server boundary.** Its OnInvoke is bound in whichever Lua VM created it, so a server-side handler is simply absent from the client's VM and every invocation returns nil. The Studio plugin's `client.invoke_bindable` runs client-side, which made the first version of this seam look wired and return null forever. A replicated StringValue has no such problem. `dm.properties` reads it in *any* context -- edit, run, server or client -- using a command that already exists, with no new plugin surface: `Command` is the write side. Set it with `instance.update` (run context) to a JSON object and the answer appears in `Result`: The BindableFunction is still created for callers inside the same VM, where it is the more direct route.
examples:
dm.properties { path = "ReplicatedStorage.ForgeDebug.Snapshot",
properties = { "Value" } }

detail.name: DeltaCounter
detail.summary: DeltaCounter — add-only counters that merge instead of overwrite. Sessions accumulate DELTAS locally; a commit pushes their SUM through the adapter's update transform, so concurrent servers never need session locks and a save from one server cannot erase another's progress. Why retries do not double-count: the local batch is cleared ONLY after the adapter reports success. A failed commit leaves both halves untouched — the store discards the transform's result, and the deltas stay pending — so the retry re-applies the exact same sum once. The one contested write is applied exactly as many times as it SUCCEEDED: zero, then one. Pure: every DataStore touch goes through the injected adapter `{ get(key) -> ok, data ; update(key, transform) -> ok, data }`.
examples:
local counters = DeltaCounter.new()
counters:add("kills", 1)
local ok = counters:commit(adapter, "player_1/stats")

functions.name: DeltaCounter:add
functions.summary: Accumulate one delta locally. NaN is rejected; anything else numeric is accepted so callers decide whether a counter may go down.

functions.name: DeltaCounter:pending
functions.summary: Snapshot of uncommitted deltas (a copy — mutating it changes nothing).

functions.name: DeltaCounter:applyRemote
functions.summary: Adopt remote truth after a load. Pending deltas are deliberately kept: they were earned before this point and will merge on top at next commit.

functions.name: DeltaCounter:total
functions.summary: Current view of one counter: remote truth plus uncommitted local deltas.

functions.name: DeltaCounter:commit
functions.summary: Merge the accumulated sum into `key` via the adapter's update transform. The transform only ever ADDS the captured batch to whatever the store currently holds, which keeps it correct when the store invokes it more than once under a write race. On success the batch is dropped; on failure it is kept intact for the retry (see the header for why that cannot double-count). With nothing pending this is a no-op that still reports success.

detail.name: Destruction
detail.summary: Destruction — things coming apart, on a budget. Every game wants breakable scenery and almost none ship it, because the naive version is a trap: a crate that shatters into forty unanchored parts is forty new physics bodies, replicated to every client, and a room full of crates is a server that stops. The interesting problem is not how to break something — it is how to break a hundred things and still hold a frame. So the whole module is built around a budget: * a global cap on live debris, oldest recycled first; * shards that sleep and anchor once they stop moving, so their physics * a fade and a lifetime, because debris that persists is debris that --- What this deliberately does not do ----------------------------------- Real fracture. Voronoi shattering of arbitrary geometry is expensive to compute and worse to replicate, and at Roblox's scale nobody can tell it from a handful of well-thrown boxes tinted to match. The shards here are sampled from the source object's own parts, so a stone crate throws stone and a wooden one throws wood without anybody authoring either.

detail.name: Editor
detail.summary: Editor — the authoring surface over a Scene. Two callers, one API. A person clicking in the overlay and an agent calling `Editor.place("Prop.Barrel", cf)` go through exactly the same operations, which is the only way the UI and the automation can stay in agreement. The server is the only mutator. Editor operations arrive as one rate-limited event and are refused unless the sender is authorised — an editor reachable by any client is a griefing tool, and "we will remember to gate it later" is how that ships. Undo is real: every operation records its inverse before applying. A place undoes to a delete, a move undoes to the previous CFrame.

Editor.place("Prop.Barrel", CFrame.new(10, 3, 0))

detail.name: Entity
detail.summary: Entity — composition instead of inheritance. The problem this solves ----------------------- A framework grows systems that know what a Player is and what an NPC is. Then you want a destructible barrel that has health but no brain, a turret that fights but never moves, a chest that can be interacted with but is not a creature — and every system needs a new special case. That is the point where a framework stops scaling and a game becomes a pile of `if`. Here nothing is a Player or an NPC. Things are entities, and an entity is whatever components it carries. `Combat` operates on anything with Health. `Movement` operates on anything with a Transform and a Motor. A barrel is an entity with Health and no Brain, and no system needed changing. This is not a full archetype ECS, and deliberately so: in Luau the cache wins of archetype storage do not materialise, while the complexity does. Component stores keyed by entity id give the decoupling, which is the part that actually matters. Instances --------- Roblox is instance-based, so an entity may own one. The link is two-way and self-cleaning: destroy the instance and the entity goes with it.
examples:
Entity.define("Health", { max = 100, current = 100, dead = false })
Entity.define("Brain",  { state = "idle", target = nil })

local orc = Entity.create({ name = "Orc", instance = model })
Entity.add(orc, "Health", { max = 240, current = 240 })
Entity.add(orc, "Brain")

for id, health in Entity.query("Health") do
if health.current <= 0 then Entity.destroy(id) end
end

detail.name: Events
detail.summary: Events — the spine everything else listens to. Why a second event system, when Signal exists --------------------------------------------- Signal connects one producer to its consumers. Events is a *namespace*: the combat system emits `enemy.killed` without knowing that quests, achievements, analytics, the tutorial and a leaderboard are all listening. That is the difference between systems that compose and systems that have to import each other. It is also what makes objective tracking generic. `Quest` does not know what a kill is; it knows how to count events matching a filter. Adding a new objective type becomes adding a line of data, not a branch in a tracker. Every emission is recorded in a ring buffer, so a playtest can be asked what actually happened rather than what was supposed to.

detail.name: Examples
detail.summary: Examples — one runnable demonstration per module. A documented example rots. It is written once, the API moves, and nobody notices until an agent copies it and gets an error. This project has been bitten by that exact shape all day: a comment describing a call that was no longer true is worse than no comment, because it is believed. So these are not snippets in a docstring. Each one is a function that actually runs inside the live game, does the thing, asserts something small about the result, and cleans up after itself. `forge example --all` runs every one of them; if the API moves, the example fails, and it fails in CI rather than in an agent's hands. --- What an example is for ---------------------------------------------- Not test coverage — `Testing` does that, and these deliberately assert almost nothing. An example answers "what does using this module look like", which is the question an agent has when it has never seen the engine and is deciding whether a module is the right tool. That is why each one is short, uses the shortest path through its module, and reads top to bottom.

detail.name: Feel
detail.summary: Feel — impact, weight and reaction. This is the module that decides whether a game reads as professional. Two games with identical mechanics, one with hitstop and screen shake and damage numbers that arc, one without — players will describe the first as "polished" and the second as "unfinished", and neither will be able to say why. It is also the layer agents skip, because nothing breaks without it. So it ships here, in the engine, as one call per effect. Camera shake here is trauma-based and noise-driven, not random jitter. Trauma decays, and offset scales with trauma squared, so small hits barely register and big ones hit hard — the difference between shake that feels like impact and shake that feels like a loose cable.

Feel.shake(0.6)                           -- trauma, 0..1

Feel.impact(pos, { color = c, kind = "burst" })

A follower is anything that trails a leader in a readable group: pets, drones, hired workers, a squad of guards. The rules are the same and none of them are obvious. What the shipped version knows that a first attempt does not: * **Small in front, large behind.** Sorting by footprint stops a huge * **Formation is a shape, not a queue.** `conga` reads as a train, * **Height needs a per-size correction.** A follower scaled up keeps the Nothing here touches an Instance. It answers "where should follower `i` of `n` stand", and the driver moves things.

detail.name: Gatekeeper
detail.summary: Gatekeeper — the load lifecycle as a tiny state machine. A profile load is async and must not block a join, so every in-memory system starts blank. A save that runs before the load resolves would clobber the real saved profile with defaults; a save after a failed read would clobber it with blanks. Those sequencing rules live here, as data, so they can be tested outside Studio — the caller keeps the DataStore access. Statuses: Pending (read in flight), Loaded (authoritative, safe to write, including "new player"), Failed (remote state unknown — never write). The failure notice is delivered at most once and only after the client handshake: a notice fired before the client connects its handlers is silently dropped and the player would never learn why progress stopped.

local gate = Gatekeeper.new()
gate:markFailed("GetDataStore timed out")
gate:shouldSave() --> "skip" ; gate:readOnly() --> true

Nudging with arrow keys is fine for a final half-stud; placing a camp means grabbing a handle and dragging it, and no amount of keyboard shortcuts substitutes for that. Built on Roblox's own `Handles` and `ArcHandles`, which render real depth-sorted 3D manipulators and give back drag distances in world units — so this file is mostly about turning those into editor operations. Three modes, one keystroke apart: move    W    axis arrows rotate  E    orbit rings scale   R    resize handles Multi-select is why the handles are adorned to a proxy part at the selection centre rather than to a placement's own model: dragging then moves the whole set together, and rotation happens about the group's middle.

detail.name: GlobalEffects
detail.summary: GlobalEffects — something is true for the whole server, for a while. Double coins for an hour. A boss is loose and everyone's damage is up ten percent. A weekend event. The shape is always the same: a named effect with a deadline, several of them at once, and every system that multiplies a number needing to know the current total *without* asking each effect in turn. Aggregates, not a list ---------------------- The mistake is exposing the active effects and letting each caller fold them. Then the payout code multiplies, the HUD multiplies slightly differently, and the two disagree in front of the player. One folded number per axis, recomputed when the set changes, means there is nothing to disagree about. Multiplicative by default, and deliberately ------------------------------------------ Two effects that each say "double coins" give four times, not three. That is what a player expects from two doublers and it is what makes stacking events feel like an event. Additive axes exist for the cases where they do not — a flat `+5 luck` should be `+10`, not `+25`. Expiry is checked, never trusted to a timer ------------------------------------------ A `task.delay` per effect is a timer that a server restart forgets and a long effect outlives. Each effect stores an absolute instant and a single sweep retires whatever is past it, so an effect is over when its time has passed rather than when a callback happens to run.
examples:
GlobalEffects.define("double_coins", { coin = 2 })
GlobalEffects.apply("double_coins", 3600, "weekend event")
GlobalEffects.aggregate("coin")   --> 2, already multiplied out

detail.name: IK
detail.summary: IK — putting a hand or a foot where the world is, not where the clip said. Forward kinematics, which is everything this engine has done so far, works from the shoulder outwards: you choose angles and the hand ends up wherever that puts it. It is exact, cheap and completely blind to the world. A walk clip authored on flat ground puts a foot six inches into a slope, and a two-handed grip authored for one weapon misses the next one. Inverse kinematics runs the other way: you name the point the hand or foot must reach and it solves for the angles. Two bones and a hinge is the whole problem, and it has a closed-form answer — no iteration, no solver, no per-frame cost worth measuring. --- Where this sits ------------------------------------------------------ IK runs *after* the animator has posed the skeleton, as a correction. That order matters: the clip still decides what the body is doing, and this only adjusts the last two bones of a limb so the end lands correctly. Running it first, or instead, gives you a character that reaches things beautifully and has no performance. R15 only, and honestly so. An R6 rig has no elbow or knee, so there is no second bone to solve for and nothing here can help it.
examples:
IK.footPlant(character, { maxDrop = 3 })     -- feet follow the ground
IK.reach(character, "right", targetPosition) -- hand goes to a point

functions.name: IK.solveTwoBone
functions.signature: IK.solveTwoBone(upper: number, lower: number, distance: number)
functions.summary: Solve a two-bone chain. Given the length of the upper and lower bone and the straight-line distance to the target, the law of cosines gives both joint angles directly. Returns the shoulder-side and elbow-side angles in radians. The clamp is the important part. If the target is further than both bones can reach, the honest answer is "point straight at it and fall short" — the alternative is a NaN from `math.acos` of something greater than one, which propagates into a CFrame and makes the whole limb vanish.

detail.name: Input
detail.summary: Input — actions, not keys. Roughly half of Roblox plays on a phone. A game that reads `UserInputService.InputBegan` and compares against `Enum.KeyCode.Q` has already decided it does not ship there, and usually nobody notices until the first mobile session shows a player who cannot dodge. So nothing in a game refers to a key. It refers to an action, and the action knows what it is on each device: Touch buttons are generated from the definitions. Declaring an action with a `touch` table is the entire mobile port for that action — there is no second implementation to keep in sync, which is the reason mobile support usually rots. detail.name: ItchAssets
detail.summary: ItchAssets — CC0 models published to this account, grouped by topic. Generated by `rqe.assets.itch_publish`; rewritten on every export. These are published Roblox Models, not baked geometry, so they load through `InsertService:LoadAsset` at runtime rather than being rebuilt from parts. That works here for the reason it fails for store models generally: the signed-in account owns them, because it published them. `textured` is the field that matters when choosing, and it is measured rather than inferred: every asset here was loaded once in Studio and its descendants counted. The obvious inference -- a `.glb` embeds its images, an `.fbx` names them by relative path and so arrives grey -- is sound about file formats and was wrong about 144 of these 295 assets, because a GLB whose materials are plain untextured colours converts to a bare MeshPart and the colour does not survive the import. So do not restore the guess. If `textured` is false, nothing in the asset carries colour and the caller has to supply it. `meshes` is how many MeshParts came out. One means a single welded shape, which is what you get from a GLB that lost its materials; several means the pack modelled parts separately, and their names are often meaningful (`house5_door1`, `house5_windows`) in a way that a tint pass can use. Every entry keeps the pack and author it came from. CC0 asks for no credit -- the provenance is for the question "what is this and where did it come from", which is asked long after the answer stops being obvious. 538 models across 63 topics, 236 of them carrying colour of their own. Published 2026-09-01.

detail.name: ItchIcons
detail.summary: ItchIcons — CC0 UI art published to this account, keyed by what it is for. Generated by `rqe.assets.itch_ui`; rewritten on every export. Do not edit. Two kinds of entry, and the difference matters at the call site. A **whole** entry is one image that is one icon. Point an `ImageLabel` at it and you are done. A **cell** entry is one rectangle of a sprite sheet -- most UI packs ship ninety icons as a single PNG, and Roblox crops one out with `ImageRectOffset` and `ImageRectSize`. That is the better shape anyway: one asset, one texture, one fetch, instead of ninety of each. `apply` handles both, which is why it exists and why UI code should call it rather than reading `.image` and assigning it. Reading the id alone works for a whole entry and silently shows the entire sheet for a cell one. Sheets whose grid could not be established are here with `cells = 0`. They are usable as a whole image and not as icons, and that is recorded rather than guessed: a wrong grid shows every icon as a quarter of itself plus a sliver of its neighbour, and looks deliberate. 348 whole icons across 77 tokens, and 59 sheets holding 9133 cells. Published 2026-09-01.

detail.name: Leaderboard
detail.summary: Leaderboard — persistent cross-server rankings that reset cleanly. `Movement.Scoreboard` ranks the players in one match. This ranks everyone who has ever played, across every server, and survives restarts. They solve different problems and neither substitutes for the other. Generalised from a shipped game's leaderboard service. Four of its decisions are the difference between a board that works and one that quietly eats a game's DataStore budget. You cannot clear an OrderedDataStore. So do not try. --------------------------------------------------- There is no "delete everything" call, and walking the keys to remove them costs a request per player and races every server still writing. The shipped answer is to **stop reading the old store and start reading a new one**: the store's name carries the start of the current round, so rotation is a string change. It is atomic, it is free, and the abandoned stores age out on their own and are never read again. This is the single most useful thing in this file. Write only what changed ----------------------- A player whose score has not moved does not need writing. Without this check every server burns its write budget re-publishing identical numbers, and DataStore throttling is invisible until the board stops updating. Read a hundred, show ten, name ten ---------------------------------- Resolving a user id to a name is its own request. A board that fetches a hundred entries and names all of them makes ninety calls nobody sees. Names are resolved for the visible rows only, and the shipped comment says why it mattered: it keeps the refresh cost bounded as the game grows. Zero is not a rank ------------------ On a competitive board a score of zero is removed rather than written, so the board does not fill with every player who has ever loaded in and done nothing. On a lifetime-total board zero is a real value and is kept, which is why it is a per-board setting rather than a rule.

detail.name: LiveOps
detail.summary: LiveOps — changing a running game without shipping a new one. A game that can only be changed by publishing is a game whose every balance tweak costs a release and whose every mistake costs a rollback. Everything here exists so a number can be moved, a feature can be switched off, or an experiment can be started, while people are playing. Four things, because they are one mechanism wearing four hats: config   a value the server reads instead of a constant flags    a config value that is a boolean, with a kill switch bucket   a config value chosen per player, which is an experiment text     a config value chosen per locale, which is localisation --- Where the values come from ----------------------------------------- A real DataStore, read on an interval, with the last good values kept in memory. That ordering matters more than it looks: a DataStore outage must never take the game down, so a failed refresh leaves the previous values in place and says so. A config system that fails closed turns a Roblox incident into your incident. --- Bucketing -------------------------------------------------------------- Assignment is a hash of the player's id and the experiment name, not a random roll. A player therefore lands in the same arm on every server, on every session, forever — which is the difference between an experiment and noise. It also means no state has to be stored to remember the decision.

LiveOps.flag("newLootTable", false)
LiveOps.experiment("firstSessionLength", { "control", "longer" })
