detail.name: Luck
detail.summary: Luck — shifting the odds toward the rare end, without breaking the economy. `Progression.CrateRoll` rolls a weighted table and guarantees a rare after enough failures. Luck is the other half of every gacha economy: the temporary or purchased multiplier that makes rare outcomes more likely while it lasts. Two decisions from a shipped simulator, both of which exist because the obvious version broke something. Luck does not stack. It arbitrates. ----------------------------------- A player with a luck gamepass, a luck potion and a lucky player standing in their server does **not** get 2 x 3 x 2. They get the best single source. Multiplying is the obvious implementation and it is how gacha economies die: sources are added over a game's life, each one reasonable on its own, and their product eventually makes the rarest tier common. Taking the maximum means a new source can never do more than the strongest existing one, so the ceiling is a number somebody chose rather than a number that emerged. Luck earned by progress is measured by *coverage*, not by volume --------------------------------------------------------------- If a game pays luck for collecting things, pay it for the **fraction of the collection discovered**, never for the raw number of rolls. The shipped game's note on this is blunt: not raw count, index -- so that parking on one source and grinding it forever stops paying luck. A count-based bonus rewards the exact behaviour a collection game does not want, which is a player farming the single cheapest source until the numbers get large. A coverage-based one pays for breadth, which is the behaviour the collection exists to encourage. What luck does to the table --------------------------- It multiplies the weight of everything at or above a rarity threshold, then the roll renormalises as it always would. Common outcomes are not made rarer directly; they shrink because the rare end grew. This keeps a luck multiplier readable -- "twice as likely to see a legendary" is true -- and it cannot ever remove an outcome from the table.
examples: local drops = Luck.apply(crate.drops, multiplier, 3)

functions.name: Luck.best
functions.summary: The strongest active source, and which one it was. Returns 1 and nil when nothing applies, so the result is always safe to multiply by. Sources at or below 1 are ignored rather than allowed to reduce luck -- an "unlucky" mechanic is a different thing and should not arrive by way of a misconfigured bonus.

functions.name: Luck.fromCompletion
functions.signature: Luck.fromCompletion(discovered: number, obtainable: number, maxBonus: number?)
functions.summary: Luck earned from how much of a collection has been found. `discovered / obtainable` scaled to `maxBonus`, returned as a multiplier. A player who has found none of it gets 1; one who has found all of it gets `1 + maxBonus`. `obtainable` is the count a player can actually still get -- not everything that has ever existed. Counting retired or event-limited entries in the denominator means the bonus can never be completed, and a bonus that cannot be completed stops motivating the moment players work that out.

functions.name: Luck.apply
functions.signature: Luck.apply(drops: { any }, multiplier: number, minRarity: number?)
functions.summary: Reweight a drop table by a luck multiplier. `minRarity` is the lowest rarity luck touches; anything below it keeps its weight. Returns a new table -- the caller's drops are configuration and must not be mutated by a roll, or two players with different luck would fight over the same numbers. Weights, not probabilities: the roll normalises, so this never has to produce something summing to one and never has to decide what to take away from the common outcomes.

functions.name: Luck.odds
functions.summary: The chance of each outcome, as a fraction, for a UI that shows odds. Worth having in the library rather than in each game's UI: a displayed odds table computed separately from the roll is a displayed odds table that will eventually disagree with it, and players notice that faster than they notice anything else.

functions.name: Luck.effect
functions.signature: Luck.effect(base: { any }, lucky: { any }, id: string)
functions.summary: How much luck actually changed a given outcome's odds. For the "your luck makes this 2.4x more likely" line. Computed from the two tables rather than from the multiplier, because the multiplier is not the answer: renormalisation means a 2x weight on one of several rare outcomes is less than 2x on the final chance.

detail.name: Mark
detail.summary: Mark — tell the Quality Engine what it is looking at. The gap this closes ------------------- The Quality Engine can photograph a place, measure its palette, check that the thing a scene is about stays visible from the viewpoints a player actually gets, and score whether a region reads. It finds all of that by **tag**: `RQEVisualRoot` on a thing, `RQEVisualRegion` on a floor, `RQELandmark` on the subject, `RQELandmarkAnchor` on the points that must be visible. A world built by `World.scatter` carries none of those. So the strongest half of the validator looked at every Forge game and correctly reported that it could not see anything — not a low score, an inability to be looked at. Two halves of one repository, each complete, unable to speak. This is the vocabulary they now share. Why tags and not a manifest --------------------------- A manifest is written once and is wrong the moment the world generator changes a number. A tag travels with the instance, so a world that regenerates on a new seed stays describable without anyone editing anything — and the marking survives `forge scene pull`, which a side-car file would not. Nothing here changes how anything looks. Every function is a label.
examples:
Mark.root(rock, "rock", "granite")
Mark.region(floor, "arena")
Mark.landmark(obelisk, "objective-core")
Mark.ringAnchors(obelisk, "objective-core")

functions.name: Mark.root
functions.signature: Mark.root(instance: Instance, kind: string, variant: string?, assetKey: string?)
functions.summary: This instance is one thing worth looking at. A root is the top of a single visual object: the rock, not its six meshes. Marking parts instead of models is the mistake that turns a scene of forty props into a scene of nine hundred, and every density and coverage number computed afterwards then means something other than what it says.

functions.name: Mark.rootsIn
functions.signature: Mark.rootsIn(container: Instance, kind: string, variant: string?)
functions.summary: Mark a container's children in one call. `World.scatter` puts its output into a folder, and marking them one by one at the call site is how half of them end up unmarked the next time somebody adds a branch. Returns the count so a caller can assert on it rather than assume.

functions.name: Mark.region
functions.summary: A named area, with a profile the spec holds to a standard. The profile is the join: the spec says what an "arena" must contain and how much of it, this says which instance is one. Regions are what let the question be "is this place composed" rather than only "is this prop floating".

functions.name: Mark.landmark
functions.summary: The thing the scene is about. What the camera is pointed at, and what must stay visible from every viewpoint the spec declares. Most places have exactly one. A place with none is a place with nothing to look at, which is a real finding rather than a missing tag.

functions.name: Mark.anchor
functions.summary: The points on a landmark that have to be visible. Visibility is cast at anchors rather than at a bounding box, because a bounding box counts as visible the moment one corner clears a wall and a player would still say they cannot see the thing. Several anchors spread over the silhouette is what makes "visible" mean visible.

functions.name: Mark.ringAnchors
functions.signature: Mark.ringAnchors(landmark: Instance, landmarkId: string, count: number?, radius: number?)
functions.summary: Ring a landmark with anchors instead of authoring them by hand. Invisible, non-colliding and parented to the landmark so they travel with it. Ringed at roughly eye height rather than scattered through the volume: the question is whether the silhouette reads from around the place, and a point buried inside the model answers a question nobody asked.

functions.name: Mark.exclude
functions.summary: Present, but not scenery: effects, debug markers, test rigs, apparatus. The spec requires a fraction of candidates to be classified, so anything that is in the world without being part of the composition has to say so, or the game fails a composition check because of a particle emitter.

functions.name: Mark.audit
functions.summary: What is actually marked in the live place. Counted from CollectionService rather than from the tallies below, because the tallies only know about this session and the question is what the place contains.

detail.name: Match
detail.summary: Match — competitive match primitives for Forge games. Everything a round-based game needs before gameplay starts and after it ends, as pure modules: the phase clock (RoundMachine), the waiting list (Queue), deterministic card rotation (CardCycle), authoritative placement regions (DeployZone), the end-of-match cascade (WinResolver) and declarative arena geometry (ArenaLayout). None of these touch Players or Workspace; the server wires effects.

detail.name: Material
detail.summary: Material — physically based surfaces. Everything this engine has rendered so far has been `Part.Material` and a colour: SmoothPlastic, Wood, Slate. Those are Roblox's *legacy* materials, and they carry no normal map, no roughness and no metalness. A rock made of them is a coloured box with a noise texture, and no amount of lighting work fixes it, because there is nothing in the surface for light to catch. Two mechanisms replace that, and they are for different things: `SurfaceAppearance` overrides one MeshPart's textures. It is how a specific model gets its own colour, normal, metalness and roughness maps. `MaterialVariant` replaces a whole legacy material everywhere at once. Register a variant named for `Enum.Material.Slate` and every Slate surface in the game — including terrain — picks it up. That is the lever worth pulling first, because it upgrades the entire world in one call without touching a single part. --- On ids --------------------------------------------------------------- Every texture id here goes through `Assets`, which refuses anything that has not been loaded successfully once. That is deliberate: a wrong texture id does not error, it renders as a flat grey surface, which is exactly the sort of silent failure that survives every static check and is discovered by a person squinting at a screenshot.
examples:
Material.define("mossy_rock", {
base = Enum.Material.Slate,
color = "rbxassetid://...",
normal = "rbxassetid://...",
roughness = "rbxassetid://...",
studsPerTile = 8,
})
Material.applyTerrain(Enum.Material.Slate, "mossy_rock")

functions.name: Material.define
functions.summary: Register a material variant. `base` is the legacy material it stands in for. That is not cosmetic: physics reads the base material for friction and density, and terrain can only carry a variant that names the terrain material it replaces.

functions.name: Material.defineMany
functions.summary: Define several, and report how many this build could actually take. Returns the count rather than nothing, so a caller can tell the difference between "PBR is on" and "PBR silently did nothing here" — which from a screenshot look identical.

functions.name: Material.applyTerrain
functions.summary: Make a legacy material render as a variant, everywhere. One call and every Slate surface in the world changes, terrain included. This is the highest-leverage thing in the module and the reason variants beat per-part appearances for world-scale work.

functions.name: Material.tint

Unsupported materials are skipped rather than aborting the rest, because a palette written against one Roblox version should not stop working entirely on another that dropped a material from the terrain set.

functions.name: Material.water
functions.summary: Water, which is its own thing. `SetMaterialColor` rejects `Enum.Material.Water`; water colour, reflectance, transparency and wave motion are properties of `Terrain` itself. functions.summary: Apply a defined material to a part and everything under it. functions.summary: Render distance per model. It is almost always the right answer for scatter, and almost always the wrong one for anything the player stands next to.

functions.summary: Stop small props from casting shadows. A shadow costs roughly what the geometry costs. On a pebble it buys nothing, and a field of scattered pebbles each casting one is a measurable share of a frame for detail no player will ever notice missing.

detail.name: Meander
detail.summary: Meander — what a follower does while nothing is happening. Why this exists at all ---------------------- A squad that holds perfect formation while its leader stands still reads as furniture. The shipped system this comes from puts it plainly: followers should drift near their slot "so they don't just stand there -- frozen statues unless they're in combat". It is the cheapest possible aliveness. No animation, no AI, no pathfinding: pick a point near the slot, walk to it, wait, pick another. What makes it work is entirely in the timing: * **It waits for the leader, not for itself.** Strolling begins only after * **Each one desyncs.** The pause between strolls is randomised per * **It surrenders instantly.** The moment the leader moves or the follower Purely cosmetic, and best run on the client: nothing here is authoritative, and replicating a wander is paying for jitter.

idling is more obviously mechanical than no idling at all.

detail.name: Migrator
detail.summary: Migrator — versioned, side-effect-free profile upgrades. Saved data outlives code. The moment a field changes meaning instead of being added, every returning profile is misread in ways that look like unrelated bugs — unless each old shape has an explicit step to the next. Migrator runs those steps in ascending order from the stored version and then reconciles the template so no field is ever nil where the game expects a value. Returns `{ data, fromVersion, toVersion }`. Profiles written by a NEWER build are reconciled but never downgraded or re-stamped — this server does not know what those fields mean yet. Pure: the input table is copied first, transforms receive the copy, and nothing here touches DataStores (the adapter owns that).

functions.name: Migrator:migrate
functions.returns: { data: any, fromVersion: number, toVersion: number }

detail.name: MissionInstance
detail.summary: MissionInstance — several parties running the same content, in one server. The problem ----------- A dungeon, a raid, a heist, a wave defence. Four players go in, and while they are in there the rest of the server must not see their enemies, their loot, their timer or their failure. Roblox gives you one Workspace, so "instanced" is something you build rather than something you get. Two ways to do it and only one that scales: reserve a server per party, or run every instance in one server with membership and visibility handled by hand. The first costs a server per four players and a teleport per run; the second costs this module. For anything under about ten concurrent parties the second wins, and it wins by a lot. What it owns and what it does not --------------------------------- It owns membership, state, the objective cursor and the lifetime. It does **not** own geometry, spawning or rewards — those are the game's, and a mission system that spawned things would be a game rather than a library. It hands out a `run` with an id; the game builds its dungeon somewhere and tags it with that id. Why the timer is checked and not scheduled ------------------------------------------ Same reason as everywhere else in this engine: a `task.delay` per instance is a promise that a lagging server breaks silently. `sweep` compares deadlines against the clock, so an instance ends when its time is up rather than when a callback happens to fire.
examples:
local run = MissionInstance.open("crypt", { leader = player })
MissionInstance.join(run, otherPlayer)
MissionInstance.advance(run, "boss_reached")
MissionInstance.close(run, "cleared")

functions.name: MissionInstance.open
functions.summary: Start a run. Returns the run or nil and a reason. The id is short and sequential rather than a GUID: it is used as a tag on hundreds of instances and read in logs by people, and `crypt#7` is legible where a GUID is not.

functions.name: MissionInstance.leave
functions.summary: Take a player out. A run that loses its last member closes rather than lingering. An empty instance holding geometry and enemies is the leak that turns a busy server into a slow one over an evening.

functions.name: MissionInstance.advance
functions.summary: Move the objective cursor on. Named rather than numbered at the call site: `advance(run, "boss_reached")` says what happened, and a mission whose objectives get reordered does not silently start firing the wrong one. A name that is not the current objective is refused, which catches the double-fire that otherwise skips a stage.

functions.name: MissionInstance.sweep
functions.summary: End whatever has run out of time. Returns what it closed. Call it on a slow loop; a mission measured in minutes does not need checking every frame.

functions.name: MissionInstance.status
functions.summary: : What a run looks like to a UI: where it is, who is in it, how long is left.

detail.name: ModerationKit
detail.summary: ModerationKit — decaying suspicion score with verdicts. Reports accumulate severity points with timestamps; the score decays linearly so old sins fade, and thresholds map to verdicts. The state is serializable, so history rides inside the offender's own save.

functions.name: ModerationKit.report

detail.name: ModifierPipeline
detail.summary: ModifierPipeline — a number, and why it is that number. What this adds over `Save.StatsDeriver` --------------------------------------- `StatsDeriver` resolves base + flats + percents in one fixed order, which is right for a stat block and wrong for everything shaped like a payout. A coin reward passes through a gamepass multiplier, a weekend event, a guild bonus, an enchant, and a hard cap — in that order, because the order changes the answer, and a cap applied before a multiplier is not a cap. Two things this has that a fixed order cannot: **Named stages, each with its own combine rule.** `add`, `multiply`, `override` and `cap` are different operations and a pipeline needs all four. A cap is not a small multiplier. **An audit trail.** Every contribution is labelled, so the output is not just `47` but the list of things that made it 47. That is the difference between a player asking "why is my damage 47" and being answered, and a developer bisecting six systems to find out. Why providers are functions --------------------------- A modifier that is a number is a modifier that was true when somebody wrote it down. A gamepass bonus depends on who is asking, a weekend event on what day it is, a guild bonus on a roster that changes. Providers take the context and answer for that call, which is the only form that stays true.
examples:
local total, why = Pipeline.resolve("coin_payout", 100, { player = id })
--> 200, { { stage = "event", label = "double_coins_weekend", ... } }

functions.name: ModifierPipeline.define
functions.summary: Declare a pipeline as an ordered list of stages. A stage is `"name"` for the default `add`, or `{ name, mode }`. Order is the declaration: stages run in the order given, and reordering them is a balance change rather than a refactor.

functions.name: ModifierPipeline.provide
functions.signature: ModifierPipeline.provide(id: string, stage: string, provider: (context: any) -> any)
functions.summary: Add something that contributes to a stage. Several providers may share a stage and all of them run; that is how a player with two gamepasses and an event bonus gets all three. A provider may return a number, one contribution, or a list of them.

functions.name: ModifierPipeline.resolve
functions.signature: ModifierPipeline.resolve(id: string, base: number, context: any?)
functions.summary: Run the pipeline, and return both the number and the story. The second return is the reason this module exists. It is a list of steps, each naming the stage, the label, what the value was and what it became — which is an answer to "why", written at the moment the answer was true. A provider that errors is skipped with a warning rather than taking the payout down. A broken guild bonus should cost the guild bonus, not the player's coins.

functions.name: ModifierPipeline.explain
functions.signature: ModifierPipeline.explain(id: string, base: number, context: any?)
functions.summary: The same answer, as sentences. For a debug seam, a support ticket, or an agent trying to work out why a number moved. A table of steps is machine-readable and a person reading it still has to do the arithmetic in their head.

detail.name: Monetization
detail.summary: Monetization — passes, products and receipts that cannot double-grant. `ProcessReceipt` is the most dangerous callback in Roblox. Roblox retries it until it returns `PurchaseGranted`, which means: * return the wrong value and the player is charged and gets nothing; * grant without recording and a retry grants twice; * error inside the handler and Roblox keeps calling it, forever. So the grant and the record are one operation, keyed on the receipt's own `PurchaseId`, in a DataStore. That is the entire correctness story and it is not optional.
examples:
Monetization.prompt(player, "small_coins")
if Monetization.owns(player, "vip") then ... end

functions.name: Monetization.owns
functions.summary: Cached, because `UserOwnsGamePassAsync` is a web call and gameplay asks "does this player have VIP" in places that run every frame. The cache expires so a mid-session purchase is picked up without a rejoin.

functions.name: Monetization.processReceipt
functions.summary: The receipt handler, callable directly. Roblox owns the real one, which makes it unreachable from a test — and this is the one function in the engine whose bug costs money. Exposing it lets a live suite deliver the same receipt twice and assert that the grant happened once, which is the failure Roblox's retry behaviour causes routinely.

detail.name: MonteCarlo
detail.summary: MonteCarlo — headless strategy simulation for balance gates. Balance claims need evidence before release: run N deterministic simulations of a strategy over the seeded rng, aggregate time-to- threshold and outcome distributions, and compare against budget assertions. Pure — runs in CI in milliseconds per thousand sims.

detail.name: MultiSlot

The rules that are easy to get wrong live here, pure and testable: how slot keys are derived, which of several loaded entries is the real one, and how to summarize slots without paying for their payloads. Suffixes spell out for the first ten slots (readable in the DataStore dashboard) and fall back to `-sN` beyond, so the scheme never runs out.

local name = MultiSlot.slotName("Profile", 2) --> "Profile-two"
local latest = MultiSlot.resolveLatest(entries)

functions.name: MultiSlot.resolveLatest
functions.summary: The most recent entry, or nil when nothing usable was given. Tie-break is stable: among equal timestamps the EARLIEST entry wins, because scanning replaces only on a strictly greater timestamp. Same input order, same winner — no dependence on hash order or wall-clock jitter.

Enough to show "Slot 2 — empty / last played Tuesday" in a picker without walking (or even materializing) the full profile.

detail.name: Nav
detail.summary: Nav — getting from here to there without walking into things. Until now every actor in this engine moved by pointing itself at its target and calling `Humanoid:MoveTo`. On a flat arena that is invisible. On any world with a rock in it, the enemy walks into the rock and stays there, pressing forward forever, which is the single most recognisable "this is an amateur Roblox game" behaviour there is. This wraps Roblox's own `PathfindingService` — a real navmesh computed from the real world, not a grid this engine invented — and adds the parts that service leaves to you: * repathing when the target moves, throttled so a chasing enemy does not * waypoint following with a stuck detector, because a computed path is * a straight-line fallback, so a failed path degrades to the old --- On costs ------------------------------------------------------------ `AgentParameters` are the difference between an enemy that squeezes through a doorway and one that refuses to. They are exposed per agent rather than fixed, because a hulking brute genuinely does need a wider path than a stalker, and pretending otherwise is how you get a boss stuck on a fence.

functions.summary: Compute a path, or say why not. Returns the waypoint list and a status string. The status matters: a caller that treats "NoPath" the same as "Success with zero waypoints" will happily report that an actor has arrived when it never set off.

functions.signature: Nav.reachable(from: Vector3, to: Vector3, parameters: any?)
functions.summary: Is there a walkable route at all? Cheap enough to ask before committing to a fight: an enemy that cannot reach the player should give up and go home rather than press against a wall until the session ends.

functions.summary: Put an actor on a path and keep it there. `target` may be a Vector3, a Model, or a function returning either — the function form is what makes chasing work, because the goal is re-read every step rather than captured once.

detail.name: Net
detail.summary: Net — a typed, validated, rate-limited bus between client and server. Roblox gives you RemoteEvent, which is a hole in your server. Every exploit that matters in a Roblox game goes through one: the client sends `{ price = 0 }` and the server believes it. The defence is not vigilance, it is making the unsafe path harder to write than the safe one. So: an event that is not declared does not exist, every client->server packet is shape-checked before your handler sees it, and every one is rate limited whether you remembered to think about it or not. Server: Client: Nothing here decides what your events mean. It only decides that they are declared, shaped and throttled.
examples:
Net.on("Attack", function(player, payload) ... end)
Net.fire(player, "StateSync", state)
Net.fireNear(position, 120, "Effect", fx)

Net.send("Attack", { dir = look })
Net.on("StateSync", function(state) ... end)
local stock = Net.request("GetShop", { shop = "smith" })

detail.name: Netcode
detail.summary: Netcode — prediction, reconciliation, lag compensation and interpolation. `Net` is the transport: typed, validated, rate limited. It says nothing about *time*, and time is the whole problem in an action game. Without this layer the loop is: which means every action costs a round trip. At 50ms nobody notices. At 150ms the swing lags the click. At 200ms it reads as rubber. With it: Four pieces, and each solves a different symptom: prediction      your own actions feel instant reconciliation  a rejected action is undone, not left desynced rewind          a hit that looked good on your screen counts interpolation   other people and enemies move smoothly, not in steps What this is not ---------------- It is not rollback netcode for a fighting game and does not pretend to be. Roblox owns the physics step and does not expose a deterministic rewind of the whole simulation. What it does is make *gameplay actions* feel local and *hit detection* fair, which is the part players feel.
examples: input -> server -> authoritative state -> client sees it

input -> predicted locally -> server authorises -> reconcile or roll back
-> remote entities interpolated behind time

functions.name: Netcode.simulate
functions.summary: Test controls. Deliberately public: the whole point is being able to set 200ms from outside and watch what happens, without a build. These were, until now, defined *inside* `Netcode.latency`. Its declaration had no body, so the parser read the next three `function` statements as its contents and the final `return` as its only statement — which means `simulate`, `broadcastSimulation` and `resetStats` did not exist until something happened to call `latency` first. That is the real reason the latency sweep never produced a number. The wiring order fixed earlier was a second, genuine bug on top of this one: even with a channel to speak on, the function that broadcasts a simulation setting was nil until lag compensation had run at least once. It compiled, it type-checked, and it was found by a scenario calling `simulate` and getting "attempt to call a nil value".

functions.name: Netcode.rewind
functions.summary: Run `fn` with every tracked model moved to where it was on `player`'s screen, then put everything back. functions.name: Netcode.wire
functions.summary: Create the netcode channel and start listening. Called at module load, not from `Netcode.define`. That ordering was the whole bug behind the latency sweep never reaching a client: * remotes are only instantiated on the server; * the server only reached `Netcode.define` inside `Fight.start()`, which * the client, which starts immediately, called `Net.on("NetcodeSim")` Under Studio's fast terrain it resolved and the sweep looked merely flaky; on a slower machine the wait expired and the client never heard a simulation instruction again for the whole session. Either way the existence of the engine's own channel was hostage to how long a game's world took to build. Wiring at load makes the remotes exist as soon as anything requires `Forge.Netcode`, which on the server is during the first line of the bootstrap. Still idempotent, because `define` also calls it.

detail.name: PlaytimeLadder
detail.summary: PlaytimeLadder — rewards for time spent, without paying people to be absent. `DailyRewardCalendar` rewards coming back on consecutive days.    This rewards staying once you are here: a ladder of milestones at five minutes, fifteen, thirty, an hour, each with something at the top of it. Written rather than salvaged ---------------------------- Unlike most of this engine, this one has no shipped antecedent: none of the production games read for it had a session-time ladder, so nothing here is somebody else's hard-won tuning and it should not be presented as such. What it does carry across is the shape of the reward systems that *were* there -- claim rather than grant, persist the claim not the timer, keep the policy pure and testable -- plus one problem those systems did not have to solve. The AFK problem is the whole design ----------------------------------- A ladder that counts wall-clock time pays players for leaving the game open on a second monitor. Every serious implementation of this eventually grows an idle check, and bolting one on afterwards is how you end up with a timer that behaves differently in three places. So `tick` takes an `active` flag and **the caller decides what active means** -- moving, clicking, being in combat, not being in the lobby. This module will not guess, because the answer differs per game and a wrong guess silently either pays AFK farmers or punishes someone reading a quest log. Two things make it usable rather than merely correct: * **Grace.** Idleness has to persist before the clock stops. Without it, * **A cap on the drift.** Once idle beyond the grace, time stops Claim, do not grant ------------------- Reaching a rung makes it *claimable*; it does not hand anything over. A reward granted at the moment of arrival lands while the player is mid-fight, mid-menu or mid-cutscene, and a grant that nobody sees may as well not have happened. The claim is also the thing worth persisting -- see below. Persist the claim, not the clock -------------------------------- Save which rungs are claimed and, for lifetime ladders, the accumulated total. Never save "seconds until the next rung": that is derived, and a derived value in a save file is a value that will one day disagree with what it was derived from.
examples:
local state = PlaytimeLadder.begin(ladder, saved)
PlaytimeLadder.tick(ladder, state, dt, active)   -- each frame or second
for _, rung in PlaytimeLadder.claimable(ladder, state) do ... end

detail.name: Prop
detail.summary: Prop — rebuild a Creator Store model from baked geometry. `StoreProps` holds specs read out of real store models; this turns one into instances. Nothing is fetched: the geometry is data in the place, so this works in a live game where `InsertService` and `game:GetObjects` do not. What a rebuilt prop is and is not --------------------------------- Meshed parts come back as a `Part` carrying a `SpecialMesh`, because `MeshPart.MeshId` cannot be written -- not at runtime and not from a plugin. Two consequences worth knowing before using one for something load-bearing: * **No PBR.** `SurfaceAppearance` is a child of a MeshPart and has no * **Box collision.** A SpecialMesh is decoration on a Part, and the Part's Everything is built anchored and non-colliding by default. A store model's own anchoring is whatever its author happened to leave, and a third of the catalogued ones carry unanchored parts -- each one a physics body the server simulates for as long as it exists. Scenery needs none of that, and a caller who wants a prop to fall says so.

local rock = Prop.build("rock", CFrame.new(0, 5, 0))
rock.Parent = workspace

detail.name: Ragdoll
detail.summary: Ragdoll — a body that stops being animated and starts being physics. How it actually works --------------------- A Roblox character is held together by `Motor6D` joints, which are motors: they *drive* the limbs to a pose every frame, and physics has no say. Turn them off and the limbs fall apart, because nothing else is holding them on. So a ragdoll is two moves, and both are needed: 1. Disable the motors, so nothing is forcing a pose. 2. Replace them with `BallSocketConstraint`s between the attachment pairs Every character has those attachments already — R15 rigs ship with matching `*RigAttachment` pairs on each side of every joint, which is exactly what a constraint needs. The whole technique is finding the pairs by name. The Root pair is skipped, deliberately -------------------------------------- `RootRigAttachment` joins the HumanoidRootPart to the torso, and that joint is what the Humanoid stands on. Ball-socketing it makes the character fall through its own physics: the root keeps trying to stand while the body hangs off it, and the result is a corpse that hovers and vibrates. The limits matter more than they look ------------------------------------- A `BallSocketConstraint` with no limit lets a knee bend backwards through the thigh, and the body ends up in a knot that reads as a glitch rather than a death. `LimitsEnabled` with a cone is the difference between a ragdoll and a bag of parts.
examples: the rig already carries, so the limbs stay attached and swing.

Ragdoll.enable(character)
Ragdoll.disable(character)     -- back to animated, standing

functions.name: Ragdoll.disable
functions.summary: Stand back up. The constraints go, the motors come back, and the Humanoid is told to stand. Order matters: re-enabling the motors while the sockets are still there means two things are holding each joint and they fight, which throws the character across the room.

detail.name: RateLimit
detail.summary: RateLimit — continuous token buckets keyed by arbitrary strings. Per-key ("userId:event") token bucket that refills continuously, so two half-windows cannot double-spend the way a fixed window allows (the roblox-infected convention). Pure: nothing here sleeps. The caller either injects a clock at construction (`{ now = fn }`) or passes `now` per call, which keeps every accept/reject decision replayable in tests. `try` spends one token and returns `(true)`; when dry it returns `(false, secondsUntilNextToken)` and records a violation against the key. `violations` reports that cumulative tally (anti-cheat fodder); `reset` wipes both bucket and tally for a key. New buckets start full.
examples:
local rl = RateLimit.new({ rate = 6, burst = 4 })
local allowed, retryAfter = rl:try("42:FireWeapon")

All ceremony stays with the caller; this module only produces a plan. Lives are 1-based: `{ life = 1, balance = ... }` is a fresh save. end

detail.name: ReceiptLedger
detail.summary: ReceiptLedger — append-only, idempotent grant history. Purchases and redemptions must survive retries. A receipt id granted once is recorded forever; granting the same id again is a no-op that returns the state unchanged. That makes the whole ledger safe to replay: a retried write cannot double-grant, and a save built from an incomplete in-memory copy can never drop or overwrite an entry the store already holds. State is a plain `{ [receiptId]: payload }` table — DataStore-serializable. Nil payloads are recorded as `true`, because stores drop nil values and the entry's presence is the point.
examples:
local ledger = ReceiptLedger.new()
local state, isNew = ledger:grant(profile.receipts, receiptId, payload)
if isNew then profile.receipts = state end

functions.name: Ledger:grant
functions.signature: Ledger:grant(state: LedgerState?, receiptId: string, payload: any)
functions.summary: Grant one receipt into `state` (nil means "the ledger's own state"). Union-reconcile semantics: an id already present keeps its ORIGINAL payload untouched — the existing record may be richer than what this call carries, so overwriting would trade a complete entry for an incomplete copy. Absence produces a NEW cloned state (callers decide when to adopt it).

detail.name: Reference
detail.summary: Reference — what a reasonable number looks like. Forge gives an agent a parts bin and no manual. Every enemy's health, every weapon's cadence, every keyframe angle and every loot weight has to be invented from nothing, and the results read exactly like numbers invented from nothing: a husk with 90 health next to one with 7000, a bow that fires as fast as a rifle, a walk cycle whose arms swing ninety degrees. This is the manual. Not templates — nothing here is a genre, and nothing here decides what your game is. It is the set of proportions that hold across every action game ever balanced, expressed as numbers you can start from and then move on purpose. --- Why proportions and not values --------------------------------------- Absolute numbers are meaningless without the rest of the game: 90 health is generous against a weapon that does 8 and trivial against one that does 200. So every entry here is expressed against a **reference frame** — a player with 100 health who deals 20 per hit — and `Reference.scale` moves the whole set if your game's frame differs. That is also why `check` is worth more than the tables. Being told your brute has 260 health is not useful; being told it takes 31 hits to kill and that anything past about 12 stops reading as a fight and starts reading as a chore is the thing an agent cannot derive.
examples:
local baseline = Reference.enemy("brute")
local weapon = Reference.weapon("bow")
Reference.check("enemy", myEnemyTable)   --> what looks wrong, and why

functions.name: Reference.enemy
functions.summary: Turn a shape into the numbers a Content file wants. Derived rather than tabulated, so a game with a different reference frame gets consistent enemies without editing anything here.

functions.name: Reference.check
functions.summary: What looks wrong about this table, and why. The most useful thing in this module. Being handed a baseline does not stop an agent inventing 7000 health; being told "that is 350 hits to kill, and past about twelve a fight reads as a chore" does. Returns a list of plain-language notes. Empty means nothing stood out — not that the numbers are good, which is a judgement no table can make.

functions.name: Reference.scale
functions.summary: Move the whole reference frame. A game where the player has 1000 health and deals 200 is the same game with a zero on the end, and every table here should move with it rather than being re-derived by hand.

detail.name: RemoteProperty
detail.summary: RemoteProperty — replicated-property PROTOCOL, transport-free. Weaver (and Knit before it) bolt a per-client value store onto a RemoteEvent Instance. This module keeps only the decision-making so any transport can carry it: the server holds a revision counter and every mutation RETURNS the ordered intents to ship, while the client replays them through ClientMirror, dropping anything not newer than what it already applied. Weaver's semantics survive: `set` replaces the default and clears every override, `revokeFor` falls a client back to the default, replicated values must be non-nil (replicating "nil" is `revokeFor`), and no-op mutations emit nothing. Pure: no Instances, no services, no yielding.
examples: [{ kind = "all" | "one", target = string?, value = any, revision = n }]

detail.name: Replication
detail.summary: Replication — sending state changes to the clients that are allowed them. The mistake this exists to prevent ---------------------------------- The obvious way to replicate a store is to send every action to everybody and let each client run the same reducers. It is one line of middleware, it works immediately, and it hands every player the whole server's state — other players' inventories, unrevealed cards, where the enemies are before they can be seen, the answer to the puzzle. Roblox clients can read anything they receive. There is no such thing as a value the client has and is not allowed to look at. So replication is not a transport problem, it is a **permission** problem, and the filter has to be decided per action and per player on the server. Actions, not state ------------------ Sending the action rather than the new state keeps the wire small — an action is a verb and a couple of fields, where a slice can be the whole room — and it lets the client's reducer produce the same result the server did. The cost is that the client must have the same reducers, which is a real constraint and the reason `snapshot` exists for the join case.

functions.summary: The store middleware that sends actions on. `send` is supplied rather than assumed, so this module never touches a RemoteEvent and stays testable: a test passes a function that records what it was given and asserts on who got what. Replication happens **after** the reducer has run, so an action rejected by earlier middleware never reaches a client, and the state the server sends is the state the server actually has.

detail.summary: Rig — characters authored in code. A creature's silhouette becomes a table of numbers. That matters for two reasons: an agent can create a new enemy without a modelling tool, and the difference between a rat and a golem becomes something you can tune rather than something you have to re-model. R6 by default: six joints, and `shape` changes the posture rather than the bone count -- a quadruped is an R6 rig with a pitched torso, which reads correctly and costs nothing. `rigType = "R15"` builds the fifteen-part skeleton instead, with elbows, knees, wrists and ankles. That exists because shoulders alone can only aim an arm, never fold one, and an archer's draw hand belongs at the cheek.

scale = 0.85,
shape = "quadruped",

On a Motor6D rig that was survivable: Roblox and Forge write different properties. On Roblox's current R15 player rig the joints are `AnimationConstraint`, both systems write the same `Transform`, and the Animator resets it to rest every single frame. The result was a player standing perfectly still while every clip in the engine played correctly into a value that was overwritten microseconds later. Measured: with the Animator present, 30 of 30 samples read identity. With it removed, 30 of 30 carried the pose. No render priority is late enough to win that fight -- the Animator has to go. The trade-off is real and worth stating: a character stripped this way cannot play Roblox `AnimationTrack`s any more. For a game animating procedurally that is the point. detail.name: Save
detail.summary: Save — player profiles that survive, migrate and do not corrupt. Three failures this exists to prevent, all of which are invisible in Studio and expensive in production: 1. No session lock. Two servers hold the same profile, the second one saves last, and a player loses an evening of progress. 2. No migration. You add a field, every returning player has `nil` where a number should be, and a dozen systems break in ways that look unrelated. 3. No retry, no BindToClose. The server shuts down mid-write and the save is simply gone.
examples:
Save.onLoaded:Connect(function(player, profile) ... end)
local profile = Save.get(player)

This exists because of a bug that cost a session: in Studio the local player joins at server start, so `Save.start()` loads and fires `onLoaded` while the bootstrap is still setting up. A listener connected forty lines later — after terrain generation, say — never hears it, no character ever spawns, and the game looks like it simply did not run. `onLoaded:Connect` has that hazard by construction. `observe` does not, so prefer it for anything that must happen once per player.

detail.name: Scale
detail.summary: Scale — how big a thing of this kind should be, in studs. The problem ----------- Asset packs share no unit. One models a sofa 271 units tall, another a fuel tank at 318, a third a whole castle at 4. Nothing about a mesh says what it is supposed to measure, and every marketplace normalises nothing, so a world assembled from several packs is a world where a chair is taller than a church. The fix is to declare a target height and scale each model to reach it. The question is where that number comes from. Why it is not measured ---------------------- It cannot be. Authored height is in the pack's own arbitrary unit, so measuring 295 models tells you the median tree is 4.2 *somethings*. There is no arithmetic from that to "a tree is about 34 studs" -- that is knowledge about trees, not about the file. Why it is not a table of topics ------------------------------- The first version was: 67 topics, two numbers each, typed by hand. It worked and it does not survive twelve thousand models, because every new topic is a new row nobody writes and the fallback is one number for everything. So the knowledge lives in about a dozen **categories**, and topics are classified into them by name. `tree` and `dead oak tree` and `palm tree` are all foliage without anyone adding a row; an unrecognised topic lands on a neutral prop size rather than on nothing. The other half -------------- Height alone is not enough, and the failure is spectacular: a bush modelled 1 unit tall and 20 wide, scaled until it stands 5 studs, becomes 100 studs across. One of those filled a third of a frame and read as a hill. So a category also declares how wide a thing of its kind may be, as a multiple of its height, and whichever limit binds first wins. A squat model then stays squat rather than reaching its target height -- which is correct. The target says what a tree should measure, not that every model is tree-shaped.
examples:
local Scale = Forge.Catalog.Scale
local factor = Scale.factor("tree", authoredSize)

functions.name: Scale.classify
functions.summary: Which category a topic falls into. Two passes, and the order is the fix for a real bug. The first version matched rule words as plain substrings anywhere in the topic. `street lamp` came back as **foliage, thirty-four studs tall**, because `street` contains `tree`: s-TREE-t. Every lamp post in the village was built as an oak. The same trap is waiting in `crate`/`rate`, `shovel`/`hovel`, `barn`/`bar` -- substring matching over natural language finds words inside other words, and it does it silently. So pass one compares whole words. A topic is words separated by spaces, and `lamp` matching the word `lamp` is what was meant all along. Pass two falls back to substrings, because compound topics arrive welded: `watchtower`, `pinetree`, `lamppost`. It only runs when no whole word matched, so it can no longer outvote the obvious answer. Cached: this runs once per prop and a thousand-prop world would otherwise walk the list a thousand times for the same dozen answers.

detail.name: Scene
detail.summary: Scene — a place expressed as data, not as code. Why this matters more than it looks ----------------------------------- A world built by a `for` loop in a server script exists only while that script runs. Nothing can list it, diff it, hand-edit it, or hand it to a tool. The moment the same world is a table of placements, all four become possible — including an editor, which is only ever a UI over this data. Scenes also make unloading real. `scene:unload()` removes exactly what the scene created and nothing else, which is what lets a game move between areas without leaking the previous one into the next.

local dungeon = Scene.create("Dungeon")
dungeon:add("Prop.Torch", CFrame.new(10, 3, 0))
dungeon:add("Enemy.Orc", CFrame.new(20, 3, 4), { tags = { "guard" } })
dungeon:spawnPoint("entrance", CFrame.new(0, 4, 0))
dungeon:load()

local saved = dungeon:serialize()   -- JSON-able; store it anywhere
Scene.fromTable(saved):load()

detail.name: Serdes
detail.summary: Serdes — binary codecs and frame batching over the Roblox `buffer` global. REQUIRES A ROBLOX RUNTIME (or Lune): `buffer` is an engine global, so this module compiles anywhere but only RUNS where the engine provides it. Codecs come in write/read pairs that advance an offset, YAN-style: Each codec exposes `size` (fixed width, when constant) and `sizeOf(value)` (encoded-width estimate; variable-width codecs measure, fixed ones return their constant). BatchWriter packs many messages into ONE buffer — per frame a u16 channel id, a u16 byte length, then the raw payload — the same batching idea as YetAnotherNet's Bridge; BatchReader walks the frames back out. Frames are never trusted: an out-of-range write asserts, and a truncated tail ends iteration instead of decoding garbage.
examples:
local next = Serdes.u16.write(buf, at, value)
local value, next = Serdes.u16.read(buf, at)

detail.name: Social
detail.summary: Social — the player's relationship with everyone outside this server. Three Roblox services that Forge had never touched, grouped because they answer one question between them: what may this particular player see, do and say, and who can they bring. `PolicyService` decides what a player is *allowed* to be shown. Paid items, random rewards and links to other experiences are all gated by region and age, and the gate is not optional — it is compliance. A game that shows a loot box to a player whose policy forbids it is a game with a real problem, and nothing in Roblox stops you doing it by accident. `SocialService` is invites. Roughly half of a Roblox game's growth is one player pulling in a friend, and the prompt to do that is three lines nobody writes. `TextChatService` is chat, and more usefully, the filter. **Any** text a player authored that another player will see must be filtered — names, signs, pet names, guild tags. Not filtering is the single most common way a Roblox game gets moderated off the platform. --- Fail closed -------------------------------------------------------- Every question here fails closed. If the policy service cannot be reached, `may` returns false; if the filter errors, `filter` returns a redacted string rather than the original. Failing open on either would mean the one time the service is down is the one time a game shows a minor a paid item or broadcasts unfiltered text.
examples:
if Social.may(player, "paidItems") then ... end
Social.inviteFriend(player)
local safe = Social.filter(text, player)

functions.name: Social.policy
functions.summary: What this player's region and age permit. Cached per player, because `GetPolicyInfoForPlayerAsync` is a web call and the answer does not change during a session. A game that asks on every shop render makes a web call per frame.

functions.name: Social.may
functions.summary: May this player be shown a thing? `paidItems`      anything bought with real money or Robux `randomItems`    loot boxes, crates, gacha — restricted in several regions `leaveExperience` links out to other experiences `trading`        player-to-player trade Returns **false** when the policy cannot be read. That is the whole design: a permission question that answers "yes" on failure is a permission question that eventually answers yes to the wrong person, and the cost of being wrong here is regulatory rather than cosmetic.

Roblox filters differently depending on who wrote the text and who is about to see it, and passing the wrong author produces a filter that is legal but wrong.

detail.name: SparseSet
detail.summary: SparseSet — add, remove and iterate a set of ids, all in constant time. The problem with the obvious structure -------------------------------------- A set of entity ids is usually a table keyed by id: `has[id] = true`. Lookup is fast and everything else is wrong. **Iteration allocates and wanders.** `pairs` over a hash walks buckets in memory order, which is cache-hostile, and in Luau it costs an iterator. Ten thousand entities iterated every frame is a measurable share of the budget spent on pointer chasing. **Removal leaves holes.** Setting a key to nil does not shrink the table, so a set that churns grows and never gives the memory back, and every later iteration walks the empty space. A sparse set fixes both with two arrays: `dense`   the ids, packed with no gaps. This is what you iterate: a plain `sparse`  id -> where it sits in `dense`. This is what you look up. Removal is the trick worth knowing: swap the removed element with the last one and shorten by one. Constant time, no hole, no shuffle. The cost is that **order is not stable** — which is fine for a set, and is the reason this is a set rather than a list. Where the technique comes from ------------------------------ Every serious ECS is built on it, because "all entities with this component" is exactly this problem asked ten thousand times a frame. `Entity` gives you the framework; this is the structure underneath, exposed on its own because plenty of things want a churning set without wanting an entity system — visible players, active projectiles, loaded chunks, anything tracked by a tag.
examples: array walk, in order, no allocation.

local set = SparseSet.new()
SparseSet.add(set, 42)
for _, id in SparseSet.ids(set) do ... end   -- packed, ordered walk

functions.name: SparseSet.add
functions.summary: Add an id. Adding one already present does nothing. Returns whether it was new, which saves the caller a `has` first — and the two-call version is where double-counting bugs come from.

functions.name: SparseSet.remove
functions.summary: Remove an id, in constant time. The swap-remove: the last element moves into the hole and the array shortens. Its `sparse` entry has to move with it, which is the line everybody forgets — and forgetting it leaves a stale index that reads a different entity's data, silently.

functions.name: SparseSet.ids
functions.summary: The packed array of ids. Returned directly rather than copied, because copying it every frame would undo the whole point. **Do not add or remove while iterating it** — a swap-remove moves an element you have not visited into a slot you already passed, and that element is silently skipped. `SparseSet.drain` is the safe form when the loop mutates.

functions.name: SparseSet.drain
functions.summary: Iterate a stable copy, for a loop that removes as it goes. The copy costs an allocation and buys correctness. Worth it exactly when the body can remove — expiring projectiles, despawning enemies — and worth avoiding when it cannot.

functions.name: SparseSet.intersect
functions.summary: The ids in `a` that are also in `b`, smallest set first. The join every ECS query is: iterate the smaller set and test membership in the larger, which is O(smaller) rather than O(either). Iterating the wrong one is the difference between checking twelve projectiles against ten thousand entities and the reverse.

detail.name: Spring
detail.summary: Spring — damped harmonic motion for numbers and Vector3. Why this exists: tweens are for things that must arrive on a schedule (a menu sliding in). Springs are for things that must feel physical (a camera catching up, a weapon settling after a swing, a health bar overshooting). Almost everything an agent reaches for a tween to do, in gameplay, wants a spring instead — and gets a better result for less code, because a spring survives being interrupted mid-flight.
examples:
local s = Spring.new(0, { frequency = 4, damping = 0.7 })
s:impulse(12)          -- kick it
s.goal = 30            -- retarget any time
local v = s:step(dt)   -- integrate, returns current value

detail.name: Stance
detail.summary: Stance — what the shooter is doing, and what that costs in accuracy. `Weapon` already models bloom: a cone that grows per shot and recovers while the trigger is released. What it did not model is the other half of every shooter's accuracy, which is *posture*. Aiming down sights narrows the cone; walking, sprinting and being airborne widen it. This is the layer that makes movement a decision. Without it a player who sprints backwards while firing is exactly as accurate as one who plants and aims, and the entire risk/reward of a firefight disappears. Multipliers compound -------------------- A player sprinting *and* airborne is worse off than either alone. That is deliberate and it is what stops bunny-hopping from being free accuracy -- the single most common way a shooter's movement model eats its aiming model. The presets ----------- Four weapon classes, tuned in a shipped shooter. Offered as a starting point for `Weapon.define`, and more usefully as a worked example of the relationships, which travel further than the values: * a **pistol** blooms fastest per shot and recovers fastest, so it rewards * a **shotgun** barely blooms *relative to its own cone* -- around a * **fast weapons bloom harder**, so holding the trigger costs accuracy and
examples:
local stance = Stance.read(character, { ads = aiming })
local cone = Weapon.currentSpread(character) * Stance.multiplier(def, stance)
tapping and punishes spraying;
a burst becomes a real choice rather than a worse version of holding it.

functions.name: Stance.preset
functions.summary: A weapon definition built from a preset, with overrides merged over it. Shallow per-table, so `{ spread = { min = 2 } }` replaces only `min` and keeps the preset's other three. A deep merge here would be surprising and a replace would make the presets useless for tuning one value.

functions.name: Stance.multiplier
functions.summary: The accuracy multiplier for a posture. `def` may carry a `stance` table to override any of the four; anything it omits falls back to the defaults above, so a weapon defined without thinking about stance still behaves sensibly.

functions.name: Stance.read
functions.summary: Read a posture off a character, so callers do not each invent their own. `moving` and `sprinting` are derived from actual velocity rather than from input, because a player held against a wall is pressing forward and not moving, and should be shooting like someone standing still. `extra` supplies what a character cannot know -- chiefly `ads`, which is a game's own aiming state. `sprintAbove` defaults to just over a default walk speed. A game with its own movement model should pass its own threshold.

Who is in which room, what the score is, whose Extracted from a game built entirely on this pattern, where the whole of both halves — server and client — is one store, a set of reducers, and a middleware that decides what crosses the wire.

detail.name: Store
detail.summary: Store — one place the session's state lives, changed only by named actions. Why a game wants this and `Data` is not it ----------------------------------------- `Data` holds content — the balance tables, the enemy definitions, the things that are true before anybody joins. `Save` holds what persists. This holds the third thing, and it is the one that usually ends up scattered across twelve modules as private tables: **who is in which room, what the score is, whose turn it is, what the countdown says** — the state of the session, which is gone when the server is. Scattered, that state has no single truth. The HUD reads one module's copy, the scoring reads another's, and they disagree at the moment somebody dies during a round transition. Held here, there is one copy and one way to change it. The rules, and why each one earns its place ------------------------------------------ **Reducers are pure and return new tables.** Not because purity is a virtue in itself but because it makes "what changed" answerable: comparing the table before and after is how replication knows what to send and how a subscriber knows whether to re-render. Mutating in place destroys that. **Actions are data with a `type`.** So they can be logged, replayed, filtered and sent over a wire. A function call cannot be any of those. **Middleware wraps dispatch.** Which is what makes replication, logging and rate limiting things you add rather than things every reducer remembers to do.
examples:
Store.reducer("score", function(state, action)
if action.type == "scored" then
local next_ = table.clone(state or {})
next_[action.player] = (next_[action.player] or 0) + action.points
return next_
end
return state or {}
end)

Store.dispatch({ type = "scored", player = "1", points = 10 })
Store.get("score")

functions.name: Store.reducer
functions.summary: Register the reducer for one slice of state. Slices rather than one big reducer, because a single reducer over the whole tree means every module's state lives in one function and every change to it is a merge conflict. A slice is owned by the system that understands it. Registering rebuilds the dispatch chain, so reducers may be added at any time — which matters for a game whose systems start in an order nobody wants to be strict about.

functions.name: Store.use
functions.summary: Add a wrapper around every dispatch. Order is the order added: the first added is the outermost, so it sees the action first and the result last. Replication goes last (innermost) so it only sees actions that survived everything before it.

functions.name: Store.dispatch
functions.summary: Change the state. A function may be dispatched instead of an action — the thunk convention. It receives `dispatch` and `getState`, which is how anything asynchronous (a DataStore read, a wait, a chain of steps) participates without reducers ever becoming impure.

functions.name: Store.subscribe
functions.signature: Store.subscribe(slice: string, fn: (new: any, old: any) -> ())
functions.summary: Hear about changes to one slice. Returns an unsubscribe. Per slice rather than global because a global subscription fires on every action in the game and every subscriber then starts with `if action.type ~= mine then return end`, which is a filter written thirty times.

functions.name: Store.hydrate
functions.summary: Load state directly, bypassing reducers. For rehydrating a client from a server snapshot, and for tests. Deliberately not called `setState`: it is a restore, and using it as a shortcut for a change is how a game ends up with state nothing can explain.

detail.name: StoreAssets
detail.summary: StoreAssets — Creator Store assets that were fetched, opened and read. Generated by `rqe.assets.sweep`; do not edit by hand, it is rewritten on every sweep. Every id here was searched for, filtered on its metadata, then actually pulled into Studio and inspected -- the part and triangle counts below are measured rather than claimed, and nothing carrying a script or an unreadable payload reached this file. `verdict` is "ok" or "caveats". detail.name: Streaming
detail.summary: Streaming — a chunk layer over a Scene. Roblox's own StreamingEnabled streams *replication*: the server still holds every instance, and every instance still costs memory, physics and a slot in the DataModel. A scene with twelve thousand placements is twelve thousand instances on the server whether anyone is near them or not. This streams *existence*. Placements are bucketed into chunks; a chunk materialises when someone is near it and dematerialises when nobody is. The scene keeps all twelve thousand placements as data — a few hundred kilobytes of tables — and the world holds only what is being looked at. Two things this gets right that a naive version does not: * Load and unload radii differ. With one radius, a player standing on a * Materialisation is budgeted. Walking into a dense chunk otherwise
examples:
local streamer = Streaming.attach(scene, {
chunkSize = 128,
loadRadius = 320,
unloadRadius = 420,
budget = 12,
})
streamer:start()

boundary thrashes a chunk in and out every tick. Hysteresis is not a
refinement here, it is the difference between working and unusable.

detail.name: Sway
detail.summary: Sway — the small motions that make a held weapon feel held. A weapon welded rigidly to a camera reads as a decal. The difference between that and a gun somebody is carrying is four cheap oscillations, and this is all four. Ported from a faithful Quake `view.c` implementation ---------------------------------------------------- Not invented here, and deliberately so: this maths is thirty years old, shipped in the games that defined how a first-person weapon should feel, and every constant in it was tuned by people watching players. What follows are the parts that matter and the reasons they are shaped that way. **Units are converted, relationships are not.** The original is in Quake units -- roughly ten to a stud -- with a player running at 320 and a bob clamped to 7. Copying those numbers into Roblox would swing a weapon seven studs. The scales below are re-expressed for studs and a 16 stud/s walk; the *shape* of every curve is untouched. * **Bob is proportional to speed**, so walking pumps gently and sprinting * **The stroke is asymmetric.** `upFraction` splits the cycle unevenly, * **There is a constant term.** `bob * 0.3 + bob * 0.7 * sin(...)` never * **The clamp is lopsided** -- it can drop further than it rises, because * **Airborne freezes the cycle.** The clock stops and the last value is * **Idle sway runs three waves at different rates** -- pitch, yaw and roll Everything here is scalar and stateless apart from the bob clock, so it runs in a test with no camera, and drives a viewmodel, a third-person weld or a held tool equally well.

reads as a machine; a footstep does not.

than passing through its rest position twice a step.

aiming at, and one that dips does not.

keeps pumping while its owner is in mid-air is walking on nothing.

detail.name: Telemetry
detail.summary: Telemetry — what actually happened, in a live game. `Debug.expose` answers questions in a Studio session. It cannot tell you that 3% of players never finish spawning, that the tutorial loses a third of people at step four, or that one error fires eleven thousand times a day from one line. This is the module that substitutes for judgement. An agent proposing a balance change is guessing; a funnel showing where players stop is evidence. Forge does not pick a destination. Open Cloud, an HTTP endpoint, a DataStore, or `print` in development — you register a sink and the buffering, batching, retry and error aggregation are handled.

detail.name: Testing
detail.summary: Testing — assertions about a game that is actually running. Every other check in this project reads source. The compiler reads syntax, the doctor reads structure, the unit tests read text. None of them can tell you whether an attack lands, whether an enemy dies, or whether a save survives a rejoin — and those are the only questions that matter. So this runs inside the live game. It drives real characters through real systems and asserts on real state. Nothing here is mocked: a test that hits a fake enemy with a fake sword proves that the fakes agree with each other. --- Why bots and not mocks --------------------------------------------- A bot here is a real `Rig` with a real `Humanoid`, spawned into the real world, moved by the real movement code and damaged by the real damage pipeline. When one of these tests fails it is because the game is broken, not because a stub drifted. That is the entire point: this suite is the thing that was missing when every genuine bug in this project had to be found by a person watching a screen. --- Determinism --------------------------------------------------------- Scenarios are given their own RNG stream and their own container, and the world is put back afterwards. Two runs of the same suite see the same numbers, so a failure is reproducible rather than a story about one afternoon.
examples:
Testing.scenario("a third hit finishes a husk", function(t)
local enemy = t:spawnEnemy("husk", Vector3.new(0, 5, 0))
local hero = t:spawnBot(Vector3.new(0, 5, 6))

t:face(hero, enemy)
for _ = 1, 3 do
t:attack(hero)
t:wait(0.6)
end

t:expect(not Combat.isAlive(enemy), "the husk should be down")
end)
Testing.run()   -- returns a report a machine can read

functions.name: Context:track
functions.summary: Own an instance for the length of the scenario, and hold it still. Anchored, because a rig from `Rig.build` is unanchored and has a Humanoid: spawned at test altitude it falls, lands in the middle of whatever someone is playing, and is deleted a second later. That is exactly what it looks like from the player's seat — bodies dropping out of the sky and vanishing — and it is the test suite doing it. A scenario that genuinely needs physics unanchors what it spawned; that is one line and an explicit decision, which is the right way round.

functions.summary: A real enemy, built by the same code the game uses. Deliberately not a stub with a Health attribute: the value of this suite is that it exercises `Rig.build`, the Humanoid, the damage pipeline and every modifier the game installed. A stub would pass while the real thing was broken, which is the failure mode being designed out.

functions.name: Context:waitUntil
functions.summary: Wait for something to become true, or give up. The alternative — a fixed sleep long enough for the slowest machine — makes a suite that is both slow and flaky. This is fast when the game is fast and still correct when it is not.

functions.name: Context:expectSome
functions.signature: Context:expectSome(items: { any }, minimum: number?, label: string?)
functions.summary: Prove there is something to assert about, then return it. The failure this exists to stop: a scenario reads "every lamp is lit correctly", iterates a list, finds nothing to iterate, and passes. It asserted nothing and reported success -- and it reports success loudest exactly when the world failed to build, which is when a green suite is most dangerous. `expectSome` makes the population itself an assertion. Put it before the loop and an empty world fails the test instead of flattering it.
examples:

for _, lamp in lamps do ctx:expect(lamp.lit, "lamp is lit") end

A suite that runs beside a live game measures a moving target: one scenario here failed a correct game because a 12Hz tick had already banked the resource between the action and the measurement. Capturing before acting turns "is it 5" into "did it go up by 1", which is true regardless of what the tick did in between.

functions.name: Testing.run
functions.summary: Run every registered scenario and report. Each case runs inside a coroutine with a deadline, because the most common way a live test fails is not an assertion but a hang: something waits for an event that a broken system never fires. A hang that takes the whole suite down teaches nothing; a hang reported as a timeout on one named scenario points straight at the break.

The alternative — returning the report to a caller — only works if the caller is inside the same Lua VM, which a CLI never is.

These are `Image` assets, not Decals. The distinction is not cosmetic and cost this repository 367 assets once: Open Cloud accepts `Decal`, reports it Approved and Active, and it never renders anywhere. What to do with one ------------------- Hand the id to `Forge.Material.define` and get a `MaterialVariant`, then set a part's `Material` and `MaterialVariant` name. That tiles by studs and takes the engine's lighting. Painting it on as a `Texture` instead stretches one image over a face and reads as a sticker the moment the part is not square.

detail.summary: ThroughputLedger — idempotent count of live dropped items. Add/remove pairs must be safe to replay: removing an unknown id is a no-op, adding twice without removal counts once. The ledger answers the only question the droppers ask: are we over the cap yet?

detail.name: Tint
detail.summary: Tint — colour for imported meshes that arrived without any. Why this exists --------------- Two thirds of the CC0 models published to this account carry no colour at all. Not because the upload failed: the packs modelled them with plain untextured materials, and Roblox's importer keeps geometry and drops that. What comes back is a MeshPart the colour of unpainted plastic. A world built from them is white. Not stylised-white -- the *absence* of a decision, which reads as a bug in a way that a wrong colour never does. And the grey ones are not a random third: `house`, `tree`, `castle`, `rock`, `bush` have no coloured member at all, so exactly the models that fill a frame are the ones missing. So: colour them here, from what they are. How it decides -------------- Three passes, most specific first. 1. **The part's own name.** A pack that modelled a house as six meshes usually named them (`house5_door1`, `house5_windows`), and a door painted like a door is worth more than a house painted one flat colour. 2. **The topic.** `tree` is bark and leaves; `barrel` is wood; `castle` is stone. One colour for the whole model, which is the honest answer when the model is a single welded mesh. 3. **Stone.** Anything unrecognised. Neutral, slightly warm, and never white -- an unknown prop should look like a thing, not like a hole. Material matters as much as colour. Brown on `SmoothPlastic` reads as brown plastic; the same brown on `Wood` reads as wood. Every entry names both. What it will not touch ---------------------- A part with a `TextureID` or a `SurfaceAppearance` already carries an artist's decision, and overwriting that with a guess is strictly worse. Those are left alone, which is why this can be run over a mixed set without sorting it first.
examples:
local Tint = Forge.Catalog.Tint
Tint.apply(model, "house", stream)   -- returns parts coloured
